quests.title: Hello Tour
quests.text: Say hello to 4 classmates. Use a different greeting each time: Hi, Hello, Hey, Nice to see you. Ask "How are you?" Write 2 sentences: "... is fine. ... is happy."
quests.teacherNote: Check that students use four different greetings and copy classmates' names correctly from the name tags, and look for is/are in the answers (Ana is fine. Pau and Marc are happy.). In a morning class you can add "Good morning" as a fifth greeting.

quests.title: Guess What I Like
quests.text: Whisper to a classmate. Guess 3 things they like: "I think you like cats." They answer "Yes!" or "No!" Then swap. Write 2 sentences: "My score is ... out of 3. ... likes ..."
quests.teacherNote: Look for the third-person -s in the last sentence (Laia likes football). Stronger students can make harder guesses ("I think you like horror films") or ask "Do you like...?" to check.

quests.title: Mixed-Up Question
quests.text: Put the words in order to make a question: music, you, what, like, do. Ask a classmate the question in the chat. Then type the question in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: What music do you like? (question word + noun + do + you + verb). The check ignores the question mark. Encourage students to answer it too: "I like ...".

quests.title: Fountain Food Chat
quests.text: Meet 2 or 3 classmates at the fountain. Everyone says "My favourite food is ..." Then ask "Do you like ...?" Write 2 sentences: "...'s favourite food is ..."
quests.teacherNote: Check the possessive 's (Pol's favourite food is pasta) and food spelling. If the fountain gets crowded, any meeting spot works.

quests.title: Morning or Night
quests.text: Ask 4 classmates: "Are you a morning person or a night person?" Ask "Why?" Count the answers. Write 2 sentences: "... classmates are morning people. ... is a night person because ..."
quests.teacherNote: Teach 'morning person' and 'night person' (or 'night owl') before they start. Check the plurals: one night person, two morning people.

quests.title: Spot the Fib
quests.text: Meet 2 or 3 classmates in the park. Each person types three fun sentences about last weekend: two true, one lie. The others ask "Did you really ...?" and guess the lie. Useful phrase: "I think number 2 is the lie." Write 2-3 sentences: one classmate's sentences and which was the lie.
quests.teacherNote: Remind students to choose safe, fun facts (food, games, places, films) and no secrets. Check past simple forms, especially irregular verbs like went, ate, saw.

quests.title: Who Has the Glasses
quests.text: Solve this: Ari, Bo, Cleo and Dani are at the fountain. Each one has a different thing: a hat, glasses, a red shirt or green hair. Bo has the red shirt. Ari doesn't have a hat or glasses. Cleo doesn't have glasses. Who has glasses? Challenge a classmate too, then type the name.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: Dani. Bo has the red shirt, so Ari (no hat, no glasses) has the green hair; Cleo (no glasses) has the hat; only Dani is left with the glasses. Fast finishers can write a similar puzzle about classmates' avatars.

quests.title: Find Someone Who
quests.text: Walk around and find a different classmate for each: someone who ate pizza last week, someone who sang a song yesterday, someone who played a video game last weekend. Ask "Did you ...?" Useful answers: "Yes, I did." "No, I didn't." Write 3 sentences like "... sang a song yesterday."
quests.teacherNote: Students should ask full questions ("Did you eat pizza last week?"), not copy the prompt. Watch for "Did you ate...?" and correct it to the base form.

quests.title: Then and Now
quests.text: Whisper to a classmate. Ask: "When you were seven, what was your favourite cartoon? What is your favourite series now?" Ask about food or games too, then swap. Useful phrases: "When I was seven, I loved ..." "Now I prefer ..." Write 3 sentences about your classmate: then and now.
quests.teacherNote: Look for the contrast between past (was, loved, watched) and present (is, likes, prefers). Students who prefer not to talk about being younger can compare 'last year' and 'now' instead.

quests.title: Make a Mini Club
quests.text: Form a group of 3 or 4. Ask "Do you like ...?" until you find 2 things everyone likes. Then invent a club name, for example "The Pizza Gamers". Useful phrases: "Me too!" "Me neither!" "We all like ..." Write 2-3 sentences: your club name, members and what you all like.
quests.teacherNote: Encourage "Me too / Me neither" and "We all...". At the end, groups can announce their club name in nearby chat; make sure every student ends up in a group.

quests.title: Would You Rather Poll
quests.text: Choose one question: "Would you rather live in the hotel or in a treehouse in the park?" or "Would you rather fly or talk to animals?" or invent your own. Ask 4 classmates and always ask a follow-up question like "Why?" or "What would you do first?" Useful phrases: "I'd rather ... because ...", "Most people would rather ..." Write 4 sentences: the results and the most interesting reason you heard.
quests.teacherNote: Check 'would rather + base verb' (not 'would rather to fly'). Stronger students can compare results: "More people chose ... than ...".

quests.title: Keep It Going
quests.text: Whisper to a classmate and start with one easy question, like "What did you do last weekend?" Your goal: keep the chat going with at least 4 follow-up questions about their answers, not new topics. Then swap roles. Useful phrases: "Really? What happened next?", "How was it?", "Why did you choose that?" Write 3-5 sentences: what you learned and your best follow-up question.
quests.teacherNote: In the chat log, good follow-ups build on the partner's answer ("Which film? Who did you go with?") instead of jumping to a new topic. You can turn it into a friendly competition: who asked the most real follow-ups?

quests.title: Best Meeting Spot
quests.text: With 2 or 3 classmates, visit at least three places in Pixel Plaza: the cafe, the square, the park, the hotel or the shop. Discuss: which is the best place to meet new friends? Compare them and agree on one. Useful phrases: "The park is quieter than the cafe.", "I think ... is the best because ...", "I see your point, but ..." Write 3-5 sentences: your group's choice and reasons, plus one different opinion.
quests.teacherNote: Look for comparatives (quieter, busier, more relaxing) and superlatives (the best, the most fun). If walking around takes too long, groups can discuss the places from memory.

quests.title: Question Designer
quests.text: Invent three icebreaker questions for a new student. Make them open (not yes/no), fun and kind, for example "What's the strangest food you've ever tried?" Test them on two classmates. Useful phrases: "This question works because ...", "People answered ..." Write 3-5 sentences: your three questions and which one worked best and why.
quests.teacherNote: Good questions start with What/Which/How/Why and invite a story rather than one word. Collect the best ones and reuse them as warm-ups in later lessons.

quests.title: Small Talk at Reception
quests.text: Go to the hotel with a classmate. One of you is the receptionist and the other is a guest who has just arrived in Pixel Plaza. Make small talk for 2 minutes: the journey, the weather, plans for the visit. No silences! Then swap. Useful phrases: "How was your journey?", "Lovely weather today, isn't it?", "Have you tried the cafe yet?" Write 3-5 sentences: what you talked about and which phrase was most useful.
quests.teacherNote: Look for friendly, polite small talk and question tags (isn't it?, aren't you?). For an extra challenge, the receptionist must find out one thing the guest wants to do in town.

quests.title: Harmless Hot Takes
quests.text: Think of a harmless "hot take": an opinion about food, films, games, seasons or school life that most people might disagree with, e.g. "Cold pizza is better than hot pizza" or "Winter is better than summer". No opinions about real people. Share it with at least four classmates and ask whether they agree. Push for reasons and try to convince at least one sceptic. Useful phrases: "I see where you're coming from, but...", "Fair enough, although...", "You've almost convinced me." Write a short paragraph summarising the different reactions you got, the strongest argument against you, and whether anyone changed their mind.
quests.teacherNote: Check that hot takes stay light and kind, and step in if one turns into a comment about a person or group. Listen for concession language (fair enough, although, even so) and real reasons, not just 'yes/no'.

quests.title: Welcome Committee
quests.text: Imagine you are the Pixel Plaza welcome committee: a new student joins your class next week and might feel shy. In a group of 3 or 4, plan a 10-minute welcome in the game: where you will meet, which icebreaker you will play and how you will include someone who doesn't like talking much. Each person suggests one idea first, then negotiate one plan together. Useful phrases: "What if we ...?", "That could work, but ...", "Let's meet halfway: ..." Write a short paragraph describing your final plan, the ideas you rejected and why.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for suggestion and compromise language. The best plans give a shy newcomer low-pressure options (whispering, games with short answers), which makes a good whole-class discussion afterwards.

quests.title: Fantasy Dinner Guests
quests.text: Imagine the Pixel Plaza hotel lets your group invite only one fictional character to dinner: someone from a book, film, series or game. In a group of 3 or 4, each person nominates a character and explains what they would ask them and why the evening would be fun. Then persuade the others and agree on one guest. Useful phrases: "If we invited ..., we could ...", "Imagine how funny it would be if ...", "I'd go with ... as long as ..." Write a short paragraph summarising each nomination, the final choice and how your group decided.
quests.teacherNote: Look for the second conditional (If we invited..., we would...) and real persuasion rather than a quick vote. Keeping it to fictional characters avoids comments about real people; steer students back if they suggest real ones.

quests.title: Rescue the Silence
quests.text: Whisper to a classmate and play "awkward silence". Your partner plays a shy new player who gives very short answers ("Yes.", "Fine.") and only opens up when you use a good technique: open questions, sharing something about yourself first, finding common ground or a light joke. After three minutes, swap roles. Useful phrases: "That's interesting, tell me more about...", "Same here, actually...", "What's the best thing about...?" Write a short paragraph: which techniques worked, which didn't, and what advice you would give someone who finds small talk difficult.
quests.teacherNote: Make it clear that the shy player is a role and not a comment on anyone in the class. Strong paragraphs compare techniques with reasons and give practical advice (e.g. ask about something the person just mentioned).

quests.title: Icebreaker Critic
quests.text: Imagine you're a game designer reviewing three icebreakers for a new class: Two Truths and a Lie, Would You Rather, and Find Someone Who. Rank them from best to worst for a group where some students are shy, considering how fun, fair and easy each one is. Then ask two classmates for their top choice and compare their views with yours. Useful phrases: "While ... is fun, it might ...", "On the other hand, ...", "Unlike me, ... thinks ..." Write a short paragraph with your ranking, your reasons and how your classmates' opinions were similar or different.
quests.teacherNote: Strong answers weigh pros and cons (e.g. Find Someone Who is structured but needs lots of moving around) rather than just naming a favourite. Briefly explain any of the three games students don't know.

quests.title: Pet Pals
quests.text: Find two classmates with a pet. Ask in nearby chat: "Do you have a pet?" and "What's its name?" Write one sentence for each classmate: "... has a ... called ..."
quests.teacherNote: Students may need to ask several classmates before they find pet owners. If few students have pets, let them write about a pet a classmate would like. Check the word order in "... has a dog called ...".

quests.title: Chocolate Scramble
quests.text: Put the words in order to make a question: "like / chocolate / you / do". Ask three classmates your question in nearby chat. Then type the question in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: "Do you like chocolate?" It is the only correct question word order. The journal accepts any answer that contains "do you like", so check nearby chat to see that students really asked three classmates. To extend it, ask them to find someone who says "No, I don't."

quests.title: Avatar Spotter
quests.text: Walk around Pixel Plaza. Find one avatar with glasses and one avatar with a hat. Say "Hi!" to them. Write 2 sentences: "... has glasses." and "... has a hat."
quests.teacherNote: Students practise "has" with avatar features and greet classmates in chat. If no avatar has a hat, accept any other avatar feature, such as a red shirt or blue hair.

quests.title: Early Bird Hunt
quests.text: Ask four classmates: "What time do you get up on school days?" Who gets up first? Write 2 sentences: "... gets up at ..." and "... gets up first."
quests.teacherNote: Look for correct times ("at half past seven", "at 7:15") and the third-person -s in "gets up". For a weekend version, ask about Sundays.

quests.title: Twin Finder
quests.text: Ask a partner: "Do you like football?" "Do you like music?" "Do you like maths?" Ask more questions. Find two things you both like. Write: "... and I both like ... and ..."
quests.teacherNote: Encourage students to ask their own "Do you like...?" questions as well as the three examples. Check where "both" goes: "We both like" and "... and I both like".

quests.title: Weekend Detectives
quests.text: Find out who watched a film, played a sport or ate pizza last weekend. Find a different classmate for each. Ask: "Did you ... last weekend?" If they say yes, ask one more question, like "Which film?" Write 3 sentences, like "... watched ... last weekend."
quests.teacherNote: Check the past simple forms (watched, played, ate) and that each sentence includes a detail from the follow-up question. If nobody did one of the activities, accept "Nobody ate pizza."

quests.title: Birthday Seasons
quests.text: Join a group of 3 or 4. Ask: "Which season were you born in?" Find someone born in the same season as you. Useful phrases: "I was born in spring." "Me too!" Write 3 sentences: who was born in which season, and who matches you (or "Nobody matches me.").
quests.teacherNote: Students only share a season, not exact dates, so no personal data is involved. Check "was/were born in" and the season words. Groups that finish early can look for someone born in the same month.

quests.title: Costumes and Chestnuts
quests.text: Ask classmates about their next celebration: Halloween, the chestnut festival (Castanyada), a birthday or any other. Find a different classmate for each: someone going to 1) wear a costume or special clothes, 2) eat something sweet, 3) watch a film. Ask: "Are you going to ...?" Write 3 sentences: "... is going to ..."
quests.teacherNote: Students who do not celebrate Halloween or the chestnut festival can talk about any celebration they like. Check "is going to" + verb, and also accept negative sentences such as "... isn't going to wear a costume".

quests.title: Quest Maker
quests.text: Write 3 "Find someone who ..." lines in the past simple, like "Find someone who visited a castle." Make them friendly and easy to answer. Then ask one in nearby chat: "Did you ...?" Write your 3 lines and the name of someone who said yes (or "Nobody yet").
quests.teacherNote: Check regular and irregular past forms and the change from statement to question (visited, then "Did you visit...?"). Make sure the prompts are friendly, with nothing personal or embarrassing. Good prompts can be collected for a later class mingle.

quests.title: Talent Scouts
quests.text: Work with a partner. Find classmates who can play an instrument, cook a meal, or do a fun trick. Split up: one searches the park, one the square. Whisper to your partner when you find someone. Useful phrases: "Can you ...?" "When did you learn?" Write 3 sentences: who can do what.
quests.teacherNote: Partners should split up and whisper what they find to each other. Look for "can" + infinitive and the past simple question "When did you learn?". Accept other talents if nobody plays an instrument.

quests.title: Cafe Logic Puzzle
quests.text: Solve this Find Someone Who puzzle. Four visitors are at the Pixel Plaza cafe: Leo, Nora, Sami and Yasmin. Exactly two of them have a dog. Leo doesn't have any pets. Sami only has a cat. Nora and Sami were born in summer; the other two were born in winter. Challenge a classmate in nearby chat to solve it. Useful phrases: "Can you solve this?" "Here's a clue." Type the name of the visitor who has a dog and was born in winter.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: Yasmin. Leo has no pets and Sami only has a cat, so Nora and Yasmin are the two dog owners. Nora was born in summer, so Yasmin is the only one with a dog who was born in winter. For an extension, students write their own four-person puzzle for a classmate.

quests.title: Have You Ever Hunt
quests.text: Mingle and find a different classmate for each: someone who has seen snow, eaten snails, won a prize, and stayed up after midnight. Ask: "Have you ever ...?" When someone says yes, ask follow-up questions. Useful phrases: "When was that?" "What was it like?" "Would you do it again?" Write 4 sentences with a name and a detail, e.g. "... has won a prize. It was for a race."
quests.teacherNote: Watch for the present perfect in the first question and the past simple in follow-ups ("When was that?" "It was last year."), an important contrast. Accept "Nobody has..." if students cannot find anyone for one item.

quests.title: Opinion Twins
quests.text: Join a group of 3 or 4 and find someone who agrees with you about each statement: 1) Pineapple on pizza is delicious. 2) Summer is better than winter. 3) Cats are better pets than dogs. Give a reason for each opinion. Useful phrases: "I agree because ..." "I think ... is better than ... because ..." "What about you?" Write 4 sentences: who agreed with you, who disagreed, and the best reason you heard.
quests.teacherNote: Look for comparatives in the reasons ("better than", "more fun than") and for polite disagreement. You can swap in any light statements your class enjoys.

quests.title: Book Versus Screen
quests.text: Find classmates who know a story as both a book (or comic) and a film or series, like Harry Potter or Diary of a Wimpy Kid. Ask which version they prefer and why. Try to find two people who prefer the book and two who prefer the screen version. Useful phrases: "Which is better, the book or the film?" "Why do you think so?" "The film is more exciting than the book." Write 4 sentences comparing their opinions and reasons.
quests.teacherNote: If few students have read books with film versions, accept comics, games or series adaptations. Look for comparatives ("more exciting than", "not as good as") backed by a reason.

quests.title: Silent or Soundtrack
quests.text: Team up with a partner and investigate: do more classmates study with music or in silence? Each of you asks three different classmates and finds out why. Then whisper your results to each other and agree on an answer. Useful phrases: "Do you prefer studying with music or in silence?" "Why does it help?" "Most people we asked ..." Write 4 sentences: your results, two interesting reasons and your conclusion.
quests.teacherNote: Partners should ask different classmates so that nobody is counted twice. Look for reporting language (most, some, only one, nobody) and real reasons in the conclusion.

quests.title: Would You Rather Hunt
quests.text: Mingle and ask each dilemma to a different classmate: 1) Would you rather be able to fly or be invisible? 2) Would you rather live 100 years in the past or 100 years in the future? 3) Would you rather give up music or video games for a year? Ask why. When you find someone who disagrees with you, try to change their mind with one strong argument. Useful phrases: "If I could ..., I would ...", "Have you thought about ...?", "Fair point, but ...". Write a short paragraph summarising the most interesting answers and saying whether anyone changed their mind, and why.
quests.teacherNote: Look for the second conditional ("If I could fly, I would...") and persuasive language. The paragraph should summarise different views and reasons, not just list answers.

quests.title: Hotel Dream Team
quests.text: Form a group of 3 or 4. The Pixel Plaza hotel needs a new team: a receptionist, a chef, a tour guide and an events planner. Interview each other to find the best person for each job: Who is organised? Who loves cooking? Who knows the town well? Who has creative ideas? Then negotiate until everyone agrees (in a group of three, someone does two jobs). Useful phrases: "I'd be good at ... because ...", "How about if you ... and I ...?", "I'd rather ..., but I could ...". Write a short paragraph: the final team, why each person fits, and what you negotiated.
quests.teacherNote: Students talk about their own strengths, not each other's weaknesses, so keep the tone positive. Look for negotiating language ("How about if...", "I'd rather...") and reasons linked to skills.

quests.title: Opposite Sides
quests.text: Find a classmate who disagrees with you about one of these: "Homework should be optional." "School should start at 10 a.m." "Summer holidays are too long." Use whispers to ask around. Then each of you gives two strong reasons, and together you try to reach a compromise you could both accept. Useful phrases: "I see your point, but ...", "What if we ...?", "Would you agree that ...?" Write a short paragraph that fairly summarises both views and describes your compromise (or explains why you could not agree).
quests.teacherNote: The paragraph should present both sides fairly before the compromise. Reward hedging language such as "to some extent" and "I see your point". You can replace the statements with school topics that matter to your class.

quests.title: Then and Now
quests.text: Find classmates who have changed over time. Look for: someone who used to hate a food but now likes it, someone who used to believe something funny as a small child (for example, that the moon followed them), and someone who has recently started a new hobby. Ask follow-up questions to find out what made them change. Useful phrases: "Did you use to ...?", "What changed your mind?", "How long have you been ...?" Write a short paragraph about the three people and why they changed, adding any pattern you noticed.
quests.teacherNote: Look for "used to" contrasted with the present perfect ("has started", "has been playing"). Keep it light: students choose what they share, and a funny childhood belief is always a safe answer.

quests.title: Fair Question Designer
quests.text: Design a fair "Find someone who ..." challenge for your class. Write five prompts that anyone could answer comfortably, such as "Find someone who has tried a sport they didn't enjoy." Avoid prompts about money, family, appearance or private information, and avoid ones that only a few people could say yes to, like "Find someone who has been to Japan." Then post your best prompt as a question in nearby chat. Write a short paragraph: your five prompts, why they are fair, and how classmates reacted.
quests.teacherNote: This builds awareness of inclusive questions. Discuss why prompts about trips abroad, expensive things or looks can leave people out. The best prompts can become a class Find Someone Who sheet.

quests.title: Animal Star Interview
quests.text: Ask a classmate: "What is your favourite animal? Why?" Write 1-2 sentences like a reporter: "... loves ... because they are ...", for example "Leo loves dolphins because they are clever."
quests.teacherNote: Check the because clause and the plural after loves (dolphins, cats). Fast finishers can interview a second classmate and compare the two animals.

quests.title: Favourite Place Poll
quests.text: Ask 3 classmates: "What is your favourite place: the cafe, shop, hotel, square or park?" Write 2 sentences: "... classmates like the ...", "One classmate likes the ..."
quests.teacherNote: Look for like vs likes with plural and singular subjects. As a bonus, the group can walk together to the winning place.

quests.title: Breakfast Breaking News
quests.text: Ask 4 classmates: "What is your favourite breakfast?" Write 2 sentences for the morning news: "Two classmates love ...", "...'s favourite breakfast is ..."
quests.teacherNote: Check third-person forms (loves, is) and food words. Any answer is fine, including funny ones like pizza or ice cream; the focus is asking and reporting.

quests.title: Superhero Self
quests.text: Interview a classmate as a superhero. Ask: "What is your superhero name?" and "What can you do?" Write 2 sentences: "Meet ...! She can ...", like "Meet Captain Pizza! She can talk to cats."
quests.teacherNote: Check can + base verb (can fly, not can to fly or cans fly). At the end, invite students to share the best superhero names in nearby chat.

quests.title: Live from the Square
quests.text: Go to the square and say "Hi!" to 2 avatars. Look at their hats, hair, glasses and shirts. Write 2 sentences like a TV reporter: "... has a red hat. ... wears blue glasses."
quests.teacherNote: Look for has/wears and adjective order (a red hat, not a hat red). If the square is empty, any busy place works; descriptions should be about avatars only and always kind.

quests.title: Weekend Scoop
quests.text: Interview a classmate about last weekend. Ask: "What did you do?", "Where did you go?" and "What was the best part?" Useful phrases: "On Saturday she ...", "The best part was ...". Write 3 sentences for the school news about their weekend.
quests.teacherNote: Check irregular past forms (went, ate, saw) and did + base verb in the questions. A quiet weekend at home is great news too: "She watched films and slept a lot" is a perfect answer.

quests.title: The Duck Exclusive
quests.text: Go to the pond in the park and imagine a duck gives you an interview. Ask it 3 questions and invent its answers. Say the funniest answer in nearby chat. Write the interview: 3 questions and answers, like: "What did you eat today?" "I ate a sock!"
quests.teacherNote: Look for correct question forms (did + base verb) and past simple in the duck's answers. Read a few duck answers aloud at the end for a laugh; it works even if no duck sprite is visible.

quests.title: After-School Headlines
quests.text: Ask 3 classmates: "What are you going to do after school today?" Then ask one more question, like "Is it going to be fun?" Useful phrases: "Pau is going to ...", "She thinks it is going to be ...". Write 3 sentences for the evening news, one about each classmate.
quests.teacherNote: Check is/are going to + base verb. If the session is late in the day, change the question to "this weekend" or "tomorrow".

quests.title: When We Were Small
quests.text: Ask 4 classmates: "What was your favourite toy when you were small?" and "Where is it now?" Useful phrases: "Her favourite toy was ...", "He had a ...". Write 3 sentences about the funniest or most surprising toys.
quests.teacherNote: Check past simple (was, had, loved) next to present simple for "now" (it is in a box). Students who do not remember can invent a toy.

quests.title: Hidden Talent Profile
quests.text: Interview a classmate about something they are good at, like cooking, drawing, a sport or telling jokes. Ask: "What can you do well?", "When did you start?" and "How did you learn?" Write 3 sentences for a profile, like: "Meet Nil. He can juggle. He started when he was eight."
quests.teacherNote: Check can for ability and past simple for how and when they started. Make sure everyone has something: listening, sleeping late or making friends laugh all count as talents.

quests.title: Dream School Day
quests.text: Interview 3 classmates about their perfect school day. Ask when it starts, which subjects they would keep or remove, and what's for lunch. Ask follow-up questions like "Why?" or "Is that better than now?" Useful phrases: "She prefers ...", "It's better than ...", "Everyone agreed that ...". Write 4 sentences for the school magazine comparing their ideas.
quests.teacherNote: Look for comparatives (earlier, longer, more interesting) and reasons behind each idea. Groups can vote for their best idea and post it in nearby chat.

quests.title: Famous in 2040
quests.text: Imagine it is 2040 and a classmate is famous. Interview them: "What are you famous for?", "How did it happen?" and "What was the hardest part?" Ask at least one follow-up question too. Useful phrases: "She became famous for ...", "According to him, ...". Write a 4-sentence profile for a celebrity magazine.
quests.teacherNote: Check past simple used from the future viewpoint and reporting phrases like "according to". Encourage ambitious, silly answers (first teen astronaut, world pizza champion).

quests.title: Great Season Showdown
quests.text: Survey at least 5 classmates: "Which is better, summer or winter?" Always ask "Why?" and remember the best reason. Useful phrases: "Most people think ...", "Only two chose ...", "The most popular reason was ...". Write a 4-sentence news report with the results and the best reasons on both sides.
quests.teacherNote: Check comparatives and survey language (most, only, nobody). The topic can be swapped for cats vs dogs or beach vs mountains to reuse the quest.

quests.title: Festival Face-Off
quests.text: Interview a classmate about their favourite celebration, for example the chestnut festival (Castanyada), Halloween, Saint George's Day or another one they like. Ask what they eat, what they do and what they like most. Then compare it with your favourite. Useful phrases: "We both ...", "Unlike me, she ...", "For him, the best part is ...". Write 4 sentences comparing your two celebrations.
quests.teacherNote: Look for comparison language (both, unlike, while). Any celebration counts, including birthdays or a town festival, so nobody is left out; students should type English names like chestnut festival.

quests.title: Game Review Panel
quests.text: Interview 2 or 3 classmates about the best game they know: a video game, board game or playground game. Ask how to play it, why it's fun and what is annoying about it. Useful phrases: "It's more exciting than ...", "The only problem is ...", "She gives it 4 stars". Write a 4-5 sentence review comparing their games and giving each one a star rating.
quests.teacherNote: Look for balanced opinions (good points and one problem) and comparatives. Board games and playground games count equally; keep any video games age-appropriate.

quests.title: The Purple Pond Mystery
quests.text: Report the big story: this morning the pond in the park turned bright purple! Invent two witnesses (not real classmates) with different theories, like a prank, a science experiment or aliens, and quote them. Post your headline in nearby chat and ask a classmate whether they would read the article. Useful phrases: "According to ...", "Others claim that ...", "It is still unclear whether ...". Write a short front-page paragraph that quotes both witnesses and says which theory you find most convincing.
quests.teacherNote: Look for reporting verbs (claim, suggest, insist) and a clear personal conclusion. Check that the invented witnesses do not use real classmates' names.

quests.title: Time Machine Interview
quests.text: Interview a classmate: "If you could travel to any moment in the past or future, where would you go?" Ask follow-up questions: What would you do there? What would you bring back? What could go wrong? Challenge their choice politely ("Wouldn't it be risky?") and see if they change their mind. Useful phrases: "If she went there, she would ...", "He admitted that ...". Write a short paragraph about their choice, their reasons and how they answered your challenge.
quests.teacherNote: Look for accurate second conditionals and how well students report a change of mind (or a strong defence). Partners can swap roles if there is time.

quests.title: Unpopular Opinions Desk
quests.text: Run an "Unpopular Opinions" panel with 3 classmates. Each person shares one harmless, surprising opinion about food, hobbies or school, like "Cold pizza is better than hot pizza". Each speaker then tries to persuade the others, and everyone votes: convinced or not? Useful phrases: "I see your point, but ...", "Have you ever considered ...?", "Fair enough, you've convinced me." Write a short paragraph summarising each opinion, the strongest argument and which opinion won the most votes.
quests.teacherNote: Make sure opinions are about things (food, hobbies, school), never about people. Look for persuasion and concession language and a fair summary of every view.

quests.title: Build It in the Plaza
quests.text: Find out what Pixel Plaza should build next. Imagine the town can add one new place: a skate park, cinema, swimming pool, library or something else. Interview at least 4 classmates: What would they choose and why? What is the best argument against it? Then try to persuade one person to switch to your favourite. Useful phrases: "Wouldn't it be better if ...?", "Supporters argue that ..., while others ...". Write a short news paragraph summarising the different views, the winner and whether your persuasion worked.
quests.teacherNote: Look for summarising language (supporters argue, while others) and hypotheticals. Collect the winners from several reporters afterwards to see what the whole class would build.

quests.title: The Advice Column
quests.text: Interview a classmate who plays an invented character with a silly problem, like a vampire who is afraid of the dark or a cat who is scared of mice. Ask when the problem started, what they have already tried and how it affects their life. Suggest two solutions and negotiate which one they would really try. Useful phrases: "Have you thought about ...?", "If I were you, I'd ...", "That might work, as long as ...". Write a short advice column: the problem, your advice and the character's reaction.
quests.teacherNote: Look for advice structures (If I were you, have you thought about) and real negotiation, not just one suggestion. Keep problems invented and silly, never personal; partners swap roles if there is time.

quests.title: Find Your Pet Twin
quests.text: Choose: cats or dogs. Ask classmates in nearby chat: "Do you like cats or dogs?" Find a classmate with the same answer. Write: "I like ... . ... likes ... too."
quests.teacherNote: Check third person -s (likes) and the word too at the end. To replay, swap the pair (pizza or pasta, summer or winter).

quests.title: Films or Games Poll
quests.text: Ask 4 classmates: "Which do you like more, films or video games?" Count the answers. Write: "... classmates like films. ... classmates like games. I like ..."
quests.teacherNote: Look for agreement: 1 classmate likes, but 3 classmates like. Numbers in digits or words are both fine.

quests.title: Me Too or Not Me
quests.text: Find 3 classmates. Say an opinion in nearby chat: "I like ..." (rain, broccoli, maths). They answer "Me too!" or "Not me!" Write: "I like ... and ... classmates like it too."
quests.teacherNote: Show one round first so students know they only react with Me too! or Not me!. Opinions are about things, never people. Stronger students can try I don't like... and Me neither!

quests.title: My Plaza Spot
quests.text: Choose your favourite place in Pixel Plaza: the cafe, the park, the fountain or the hotel. Go there. Say in nearby chat: "I like the ... because ..." Write it in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: A gentle first quest for shy students, because they only post one sentence. Check for the before the place and a simple reason after because. Encourage others to reply Me too!

quests.title: Bird or Fish Day
quests.text: Whisper to a partner: "For one day, do you want to be a bird or a fish? Why?" Then you answer. Write: "My partner wants to be a ... because ..."
quests.teacherNote: Look for wants with he/she and a reason with can (birds can fly, fish can swim). To replay, change the animals (a cat or a horse).

quests.title: Beach or Mountains
quests.text: Find 3 classmates. Ask: "Would you rather spend a day at the beach or in the mountains? What are you going to do there?" Useful phrases: "Two of them would rather...", "One classmate is going to..." Write 3 sentences about their answers.
quests.teacherNote: Check would rather + base verb (not would rather to) and going to for plans. It is framed as a day out, so nobody compares real holidays. Swap in a city or a farm for variety.

quests.title: Guess the Cafe Winner
quests.text: Go to the cafe. Would people rather have hot chocolate or a milkshake? Guess the winner first. Then ask 5 classmates and count the votes. Write 3 sentences: "I guessed ... . ... people chose hot chocolate and ... chose milkshake. My guess was right/wrong."
quests.teacherNote: Look for past simple forms (guessed, chose, was). Because students guess first, this is more than a plain poll. Change the drinks (lemonade or smoothie) to reuse it.

quests.title: Time Machine Ticket
quests.text: Jump into a time machine! Ask a partner: "Would you rather visit the time of the dinosaurs or the year 3000? What are you going to see there?" Then answer the same questions. Useful phrases: "My partner would rather...", "I'm going to see..." Write 2-3 sentences about your two choices.
quests.teacherNote: Check going to + verb and would rather + verb. Fast pairs can add one more question, such as Who are you going to meet?

quests.title: Hotel or Tent Night
quests.text: Imagine you can sleep one night in Pixel Plaza. Would you rather sleep in the hotel or in a tent in the park? Visit both places. Post your choice in nearby chat and see who agrees. Write 2-3 sentences: "I would rather sleep in ... because ... . ... classmates agree with me."
quests.teacherNote: Check would rather + base verb and a clear reason. If nobody agrees, that is fine: 0 or no classmates is a correct answer and practises the negative.

quests.title: Rainy Day Plan
quests.text: Pretend it's raining in Pixel Plaza! Meet 2 or 3 classmates at the fountain and choose a dry place together: the cafe, the shop or the hotel. Everyone suggests one place. Useful phrases: "Let's go to...", "I'd rather go to...", "Good idea!" Write 3 sentences: who suggested what and what you decided.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for suggestion language in the chat and past simple in the report (suggested, decided, chose). As a reward, groups can walk to their chosen place together.

quests.title: Music or Series
quests.text: Ask a partner: "Would you rather live for a month without music or without films and series?" Listen to their choice, then ask two follow-up questions, like "What would you miss most?" or "How would you spend the free time?" Then swap roles. Useful phrases: "I'd choose... because...", "For me, ... is more important than...", "Really? Why?" Write 4 sentences comparing your answer and your partner's answer.
quests.teacherNote: Look for real follow-up questions and comparatives such as more important than. To reuse it, swap the options (sport or video games).

quests.title: Plaza Poll Reporter
quests.text: Be a reporter! Pick one question: "Would you rather talk to animals or speak every language?" or "Would you rather have a pet dragon or a pet robot?" Ask at least 5 classmates and note their reasons. Useful phrases: "Most people chose...", "Only one person...", "The most interesting reason was..." Write 4-5 sentences: the results, the most popular reason and the most surprising one.
quests.teacherNote: Check quantifiers (most, some, only one, nobody) and superlatives in the summary. Students may write their own question if it is kind and works as a would-you-rather.

quests.title: Teleport or Freeze Time
quests.text: Get together with 2 or 3 classmates. Each person chooses: "Would you rather teleport anywhere or stop time for one hour a day?" Then everyone explains what they would do with the power. Ask each other one question about the problems it could cause. Useful phrases: "If I could..., I would...", "That sounds useful, but...", "What would happen if...?" Write 4-5 sentences about the group's choices and the best idea.
quests.teacherNote: Look for the second conditional (If I could..., I would...) and polite challenges. Remind groups to give everyone a turn before they write.

quests.title: Hotel Pet Mystery
quests.text: Solve the hotel mystery! 24 guests voted for a hotel pet: a parrot, a rabbit or a goldfish. Everyone voted once. The parrot got 9 votes. The rabbit got twice as many votes as the goldfish. Which pet won? Whisper the puzzle to a classmate and check if you agree. Useful phrases: "How many votes did ... get?", "I think ... won because..." Type the name of the winning pet.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: the rabbit. 24 - 9 = 15 votes for the rabbit and goldfish together; the rabbit has twice as many, so goldfish 5 and rabbit 10, which beats the parrot's 9 (many students guess parrot at first).

quests.title: Hot Take Showdown
quests.text: Meet 2 or 3 classmates in the square. Each person posts one fun hot take (a surprising opinion) in nearby chat about food, school, sport or films, for example "Pineapple on pizza is delicious" or "Maths is the best subject". Everyone else agrees or disagrees with a reason. Keep it friendly! Useful phrases: "I totally agree because...", "I see your point, but...", "No way! I think..." Write 4 sentences: which hot take split the group most and what people said.
quests.teacherNote: Hot takes must be about things, never about classmates or real people; moderate the chat if needed. Look for polite disagreement (I see your point, but...).

quests.title: Change My Mind
quests.text: Find a partner and, in whisper chat, agree on a dilemma where you choose different sides, for example "Would you rather live in a big city or a small village?" or "Would you rather have a talking dog or a robot best friend?" Take turns: each of you gets three messages to persuade the other to switch sides. Use a new reason each time. Useful phrases: "Think about it this way...", "I see your point, but...", "Wouldn't it be better if...?" Write a short paragraph: each person's main arguments, the strongest one, and whether anyone changed their mind.
quests.teacherNote: Assess the variety and quality of the arguments and softened persuasion (Wouldn't it be better if...?). If a pair agrees on everything, one partner argues the opposite side for practice.

quests.title: Desert Island Deal
quests.text: Form a group of 3 or 4. Imagine you are stuck on a tiny island for a week and can take only three things: a tent, a fishing rod, a guitar, a football, a big box of chocolate, a first-aid kit, a torch or a book of jokes. First, choose your own three in secret. Then negotiate in nearby chat until the whole group agrees on one list. Useful phrases: "I could accept... if we also take...", "Let's meet halfway.", "I'm willing to give up..." Write a short paragraph: your final list, what each person gave up and the hardest decision.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for conditional bargaining (I could accept... if...) and compromise. A good paragraph explains the trade-offs, not just the final list. Torch is British English for flashlight.

quests.title: Plaza Makeover Vote
quests.text: Report on the big town vote! Pixel Plaza has space for one new attraction: a skate park, an outdoor cinema or a climbing wall. Interview at least 5 classmates: which would they choose, why, and what could be the downside? Try to find someone who disagrees with the majority. Useful phrases: "The majority felt that...", "Some argued that..., whereas others...", "Only a few..." Write a short paragraph like a news report: the winner, the main arguments on each side and one view that surprised you.
quests.teacherNote: Look for reporting verbs, contrast linkers (whereas, while, however) and a balanced summary that includes the minority view. Change the three attractions to suit your class.

quests.title: The Homework Deal
quests.text: Form a group of 3 or 4 and discuss: "Would you rather have no homework ever but stay at school until 6 pm, or finish at 1 pm but have homework every day?" Don't just vote: look for answers that start with "It depends". Ask questions like "What if you had a club in the evening?" or "Would it be different in exam weeks?" Useful phrases: "It depends on...", "On the one hand..., on the other hand...", "In that case, I'd..." Write a short paragraph summarising the different views in your group and the conditions that could change someone's mind.
quests.teacherNote: The best answers go further than a vote and explain conditions (It depends on..., In that case...). Keep the talk on the hypothetical, not on real teachers or subjects.

quests.title: Devil's Advocate
quests.text: Choose a would-you-rather dilemma you feel strongly about, for example "always be too hot or always be too cold" or "live in a castle or on a boat". Now argue for the side you did not choose: find the three best reasons, even if you don't believe them. Post your strongest reason in nearby chat and ask if anyone finds it convincing. Useful phrases: "Admittedly...", "A strong point in its favour is..." Write a short paragraph: your real choice, the best arguments for the other side, and whether arguing against yourself changed your view.
quests.teacherNote: Look for concession language (admittedly, although, even so) and reasons that really support the opposite side. Ask the class to keep replies in chat friendly and to the point.

quests.title: Team Cat or Team Dog
quests.text: Ask 4 classmates: "Cats or dogs?" Count the answers. Tell them your answer too. Write 2 sentences: "... classmates like cats and ... like dogs. I like ... because ..."
quests.teacherNote: Check that the numbers add up to 4 and that the reason uses because. Fast finishers can ask more classmates and find the class winner.

quests.title: The Pineapple Pizza Problem
quests.text: Ask a classmate: "Pineapple on pizza: yes or no?" Then say "I agree." or "Sorry, I don't agree." Write 2 sentences: "My partner says ... . I agree / don't agree because ..."
quests.teacherNote: Look for the polite "Sorry, I don't agree" instead of "No!" or "You're wrong". You can change the food question, for example ketchup on chips or milk in cereal first.

quests.title: Spot the Rude One
quests.text: Read: "I agree." "Good idea!" "You are wrong." "That's true." One phrase is not polite. Whisper a polite one to a classmate. Then type the phrase that is not polite.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: "You are wrong." It sounds rude because it is about the person, not the idea. Show softer options like "I'm not sure" or "Sorry, I don't agree".

quests.title: Ice Cream Vote
quests.text: Meet 3 classmates at the cafe. Ask: "Chocolate, vanilla or strawberry?" Find your group's favourite ice cream. Write 2 sentences: "Our group likes ... best. I like ... because ..."
quests.teacherNote: If there is a tie, students can ask one more person or try a friendly "Please choose chocolate!". Any flavour is fine; the goal is asking, answering and reporting.

quests.title: Opinion Twins
quests.text: Ask 4 or more classmates: "What is the best day of the week?" Find someone with the same answer. Write 2 sentences: "... and I both like ... . We like it because ..."
quests.teacherNote: Students write their twin's avatar name in the first gap. If nobody agrees, accept "Nobody agrees with me! I like ... because ...". Check capital letters on the days.

quests.title: Uniform or No Uniform
quests.text: Ask 4 classmates: "Should students wear a school uniform? Why?" Listen to their reasons. Useful phrases: "I think...", "It's better because...", "Really? Why?" Write 3 sentences: how many said yes, how many said no, and the best reason you heard.
quests.teacherNote: Look for past simple when they report ("Three people said yes"). Many schools in Catalonia have no uniform, so most students are imagining it; collect the best reasons for a short class discussion.

quests.title: The Homework Deal
quests.text: Find a partner. One of you wants homework every day; the other wants no homework at all. Talk and find a deal you both like, for example homework only on Mondays. Useful phrases: "What about...?", "OK, but...", "Deal!" Write 3 sentences: your idea, your partner's idea and your final deal.
quests.teacherNote: Students only play a side, so they don't need to believe it. Look for suggestions with "What about...?" and a clear final deal that gives something to both sides.

quests.title: Mystery Peace Word
quests.text: Solve the riddle: "Two friends disagree. They both give a little and find an answer in the middle. What is it called?" Hint: it has 10 letters, starts with C, and the word "promise" is inside it. Use the word in a chat message to a classmate, then type it here.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: compromise (com + promise). Ask a few students to share their chat sentences, for example "Let's make a compromise: pizza today, pasta tomorrow."

quests.title: The Book Was Better
quests.text: Meet 2 or 3 classmates. Think of a story that is a book and a film, for example Harry Potter. Ask: "Did you read the book or watch the film first? Which was better?" Useful phrases: "I preferred the...", "The film was more exciting than..." Write 3 sentences about your group's answers.
quests.teacherNote: If a group knows no book-and-film pairs, let them compare a video game and its film or a comic and its cartoon. Look for past simple questions and "more ... than".

quests.title: Beach or Mountains
quests.text: Plan a dream day trip with 2 or 3 classmates: beach or mountains? Each person gives one reason, then vote. Useful phrases: "We're going to...", "At the beach we can...", "I prefer the mountains because..." Write 3 sentences: where your group is going to go, why, and one reason for the other place.
quests.teacherNote: Check "going to" for the plan and "because" for reasons. You can reuse it with other choices: city or countryside, camping or a hotel.

quests.title: Superpower Showdown
quests.text: Debate with a partner: which superpower is better, flying or being invisible? Take one side each and give two reasons why yours is more useful. Ask at least one follow-up question. Useful phrases: "Flying is more useful than ... because ...", "But what about ...?", "That's a good point, but ..." Write 4 sentences: both sides, the strongest reason you heard, and if anyone changed their mind.
quests.teacherNote: Look for comparatives (more useful than, faster than) and real follow-up questions. Fast pairs can try a new pair of powers: super strength or talking to animals.

quests.title: Fountain Season Puzzle
quests.text: Solve the puzzle. Four friends at the fountain are debating the best season, and each one chooses a different season. Tom loves orange leaves falling from the trees. Zoe's favourite season starts in March. Lia says snow is boring. Max hates the beach. Which season does Max choose? Whisper your answer and your reasons to a classmate and ask if they agree. Useful phrases: "It can't be ... because ...", "So it must be ..." Then type the season.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: winter. Tom chooses autumn and Zoe chooses spring; Lia can't choose winter, so she chooses summer, and Max (who hates the beach) gets winter. Check that the whispered reasoning uses can't and must.

quests.title: Plaza Makeover
quests.text: Imagine the mayor of Pixel Plaza can build one new thing: a skate park, a cinema or a swimming pool. Ask at least 4 classmates which they want and why, and ask a follow-up question each time. Useful phrases: "Which one would you choose?", "Why is that better than ...?", "I see what you mean." Write 4 sentences: the most popular choice, two different reasons you heard, and your own opinion.
quests.teacherNote: Look for real follow-up questions, not just one-word answers. Afterwards you can play the mayor, collect the results and announce the winner.

quests.title: Rainy Day Ranking
quests.text: Work with 2 or 3 classmates. It's a rainy Saturday: which is the best activity, video games, board games, watching a film or reading a book? Agree on a ranking from 1 to 4, and everyone must give at least one reason. Useful phrases: "Board games are more fun than ... because ...", "I'm not sure about that.", "OK, let's put ... second." Write 4 sentences: your group's ranking and the reasons for first and last place.
quests.teacherNote: Ranking forces negotiation, so listen for polite disagreement and superlatives (the most fun, the best). Change the four options to suit the class, for example sports, music, cooking or drawing.

quests.title: Early Bird or Night Owl
quests.text: Find out if your partner is an early bird (loves mornings) or a night owl (loves evenings). Ask at least two follow-up questions about their weekends or breakfast. Then debate: which is better for a student, and why? Useful phrases: "What time do you usually ...?", "Mornings are better because ...", "That makes sense, but ..." Write 4 sentences: what you learned about your partner, both opinions, and who was more persuasive.
quests.teacherNote: Good practice for adverbs of frequency and time expressions. Students only share routine details they are happy to share.

quests.title: Pets in the Hotel
focus: Conditions with as long as and what if
quests.text: Role-play with a partner at the Pixel Plaza hotel. One of you is the manager, who wants to ban all pets because of noise and mess. The other is a guest who wants to stay with a very well-behaved cat. The guest must persuade; the manager must protect the other guests. Try to reach a deal with conditions, for example special pet rooms. Useful phrases: "I understand your concern, but ...", "What if we ...?", "I could accept that, as long as ..." Write a short paragraph summarising both positions, the deal you reached and whether you think it is fair.
quests.teacherNote: Pairs can swap roles and repeat it with a dog or a parrot. Look for conditions (as long as, provided that, if ... then) and a summary that presents both sides fairly.

quests.title: The Judge's Verdict
quests.text: Form a group of three or four: two debaters and one or two judges. Topic: "School should start at 10 a.m." One debater argues for and one against, with about three chat messages each. The judges ask each side one tricky question, then decide who was more convincing. If you have time, swap roles with a new topic, for example "Summer holidays should be shorter". Useful phrases: "Even if that's true, ...", "The main advantage is ...", "On balance, I think ..." Write a short paragraph summarising both sides and the verdict, with reasons.
quests.teacherNote: The judge role trains listening and summarising. Check that the verdict refers to the arguments, not to who is more popular.

quests.title: Change My Mind
quests.text: Choose a fun, slightly unusual opinion, for example "Cereal is a great dinner" or "Rainy days are better than sunny ones". Try to persuade at least four classmates. Listen to each person's objection and answer it politely. Count how many people you convinced, even a little. Useful phrases: "Hear me out ...", "I see your point, but have you considered ...?", "Wouldn't it be great if ...?" Write a short paragraph: your opinion, the strongest objection you heard, your best argument, and how many people changed their mind.
quests.teacherNote: Make sure opinions stay light and are about things, not people. Listen for counter-arguments and softening language (have you considered, that may be true, but).

quests.title: Time Machine Tickets
quests.text: Pretend a time machine in the hotel lobby offers you one ticket: 200 years into the past or 200 years into the future, for one week only. Discuss with a partner which ticket you would take and try to persuade them to come with you. Think about what you would see, learn and miss. Useful phrases: "If I went to the future, I'd ...", "The risk is that ...", "I'd rather ... because ..." Write a short paragraph comparing your views and saying which ticket you chose together, or why you couldn't agree.
quests.teacherNote: The target structure is the second conditional (If I went ..., I would ...). For a stronger class, add a third choice: staying in the present.

quests.title: Desert Island Deal
quests.text: Imagine you and 2 or 3 classmates are on a desert island for a week (don't worry, a boat is coming!). You can only keep three of these: a tent, a football, a guitar, a fishing rod, a torch, a huge box of chocolates, a joke book. Each person persuades the group to keep one item. Negotiate until you all agree. Useful phrases: "Without a ..., we'd ...", "I'll agree to ... if you agree to ...", "Let's meet halfway." Write a short paragraph: your final three items, the item that caused the biggest disagreement, and how you reached a compromise.
quests.teacherNote: There is no right answer. Reward bargaining language (I'll agree to ... if ...) and a clear summary of who wanted what and why.

quests.title: Fish in the Fountain
quests.text: Tell a fish story with a classmate. You start: "A little fish lives in the fountain." Take turns adding sentences, like "The fish likes ...". Write your two favourite sentences from the story.
quests.teacherNote: Check present simple with third person -s (lives, likes, swims). Fast pairs can give their story a title and share it in nearby chat.

quests.title: Mix-and-Match Hero
quests.text: Ask three classmates for ideas: a funny name, an animal, a place in town. Make one silly sentence with all three and share it in the chat. Write it: "... is a ... and lives in the ...".
quests.teacherNote: Expect sentences like "Bobo is a penguin and lives in the hotel." Remind students to use invented names, not classmates' names, and to thank the classmates who helped.

quests.title: The Magic Hat
quests.text: Make a tiny story: "In the shop, there is a magic hat. When you wear it, you can ..." Post it in nearby chat and ask: "Do you like it?" Write your two sentences.
quests.teacherNote: Look for "there is" and "can" + base verb. Classmates often reply with their own magic hat idea, so it works well as a chain warm-up.

quests.title: The Hungry Robot
quests.text: Ask four classmates: "A robot is in the cafe. What does it eat?" Choose the funniest answer. Write: "The robot eats ... . I like this answer because ..."
quests.teacherNote: Practises "What does it eat?" and third person -s (eats). In a small class, two or three answers are enough.

quests.title: Avatar Story Hero
quests.text: Choose a classmate with a hat, glasses or a cool shirt. Ask: "Can your avatar be my story hero? Where does it go every day?" Write two sentences: "... has a ... . Every day, ... goes to the ..."
quests.teacherNote: Check "has" for descriptions and third person -s (goes, plays). Descriptions must stay about the avatar's clothes and accessories, never the real person.

quests.title: The Strange Hotel Guest
quests.text: Make a story chain with two or three classmates in nearby chat. Start with: "Yesterday, a very strange guest arrived at the hotel." Each person adds one sentence in the past simple. Go around the group two times. Useful phrases: "Then ...", "After that ...", "Suddenly ...". Write the best three sentences from your story.
quests.teacherNote: Look for regular and irregular past forms (arrived, went, saw, took). If a group finishes early, ask them to add a title and a funny last line.

quests.title: Snowball Story
quests.text: Write a short sentence, like "A cat ate a cake." Whisper it to a classmate and ask: "Can you add a detail, like a colour or a place?" They whisper back a longer sentence. Send it to another classmate for another detail. Do this with four classmates. Write your first and final sentences.
quests.teacherNote: The final sentence should be much longer, e.g. "On Monday, a fat orange cat ate a chocolate cake in the cafe." Check adjective order and where the time and place phrases go.

quests.title: Treasure Hunt Plans
quests.text: Imagine you and a classmate are explorers looking for treasure in Pixel Plaza. Plan tomorrow's adventure in the chat. Take turns adding one plan each. Useful phrases: "First, we're going to ...", "Then we're going to ...", "Finally, we're going to ...". Write 3 sentences about your plan.
quests.teacherNote: Check "going to" + base verb and the sequencers. To extend it, the pair can visit the places and report what they found in the past simple.

quests.title: Who Wrote Sentence Three?
quests.text: Solve this puzzle. Five friends each wrote one sentence of a story. Nora wrote the first sentence. Mia wrote before Max. Leo wrote after Max. Sam wrote after Leo. Who wrote the third sentence? Whisper the puzzle to a classmate and compare answers. Type the name.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: Max. Nora is first, and the clues give Mia, then Max, then Leo, then Sam for sentences 2 to 5, so Max wrote sentence three.

quests.title: Fairy Tale Remix
quests.text: Choose a famous fairy tale with two or three classmates, like Cinderella or The Three Little Pigs. Move it to Pixel Plaza! Each person changes one thing: a place, a character or the ending. Useful phrases: "In our story, ... lived in the ...", "At the end, ...". Write 3 sentences about your new story.
quests.teacherNote: Expect sentences like "In our story, Cinderella worked at the cafe and lost her shoe on the bridge." Any well-known story or film is fine if students prefer it.

quests.title: Pigeon Plot Twists
quests.text: Tell a story with two or three classmates in nearby chat. Start: "One morning, all the pigeons in the square started speaking English." Take turns adding a surprising twist that begins with "Suddenly," or "But then". Go around twice. Then vote for the best twist (not your own!). Useful phrases: "I vote for ... because ...", "It was the most surprising because ...". Write 4-5 sentences: a short version of the story, which twist won and why.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for past simple for events and past continuous for background (People were drinking coffee when...). If time is short, go around once only.

quests.title: Interview the Villain
quests.text: Role-play an interview with a classmate. One of you is the cheeky duck who stole all the sandwiches in the park. The other is a reporter for the Pixel Plaza News. The reporter asks at least five questions, with a follow-up for each answer. Useful phrases: "Why did you ...?", "Really? What happened next?", "How did you feel when ...?". Write 4 sentences for a news report about the duck.
quests.teacherNote: Check past question forms (Why did you take...?) and that follow-ups react to the answer rather than being a list. Pairs can swap roles with a new villain, e.g. the cat who ate the hotel's cake.

quests.title: New Character Wanted
quests.text: Find a new character for a story set in Pixel Plaza (not a real person)! Ask four classmates: "What new character should come to town, and why?" Ask one follow-up question about each idea. Compare the ideas and choose the best one. Useful phrases: "I think ... would be funnier because ...", "This idea is more original than ...". Write 4-5 sentences: the ideas you heard, which one you chose and why.
quests.teacherNote: Look for comparatives with reasons (funnier, more original than). Students can share the winning character in nearby chat to see if the class agrees.

quests.title: Lola's Lost Hat
quests.text: Put this mixed-up story in order: "Finally, she found it under a table in the cafe." "One morning, Lola lost her favourite hat in the square." "After that, she looked in the hotel, but it wasn't there." "First, she looked in the fountain." Whisper the story in the correct order to a classmate and see if they agree. Where did Lola look second? Type the place.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: the hotel. The correct order is One morning (square), First (fountain), After that (hotel), Finally (cafe), so the fountain is the first place she looked and the hotel the second.

quests.title: Battle of the Endings
quests.text: Read this story start with a classmate: "A mysterious suitcase appeared on the little bridge in the park. Suddenly, it started to sing." You and your partner each write a different ending (2-3 sentences) in the chat. Then compare: which ending is funnier, more surprising or more original? Useful phrases: "Your ending is funnier than mine because ...", "I prefer ... because ...". Write 4-5 sentences: both endings, which one you prefer and why.
quests.teacherNote: Look for comparatives and real reasons, not just "I like it". Pairs can post the winning ending in nearby chat for others to vote on.

quests.title: The Writers' Room
quests.text: Form a team with two or three classmates: you are the writers of a new TV series set in Pixel Plaza. Each person pitches one idea for the first episode: a main character, a problem and a twist. Then negotiate one plot that includes something from everyone's idea. Rule: nobody can reject an idea without suggesting an alternative. Useful phrases: "What if we combined ...?", "I see your point, but ...", "Would you be happy if ...?". Write a short paragraph summarising the final plot and the compromises your group made.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for polite disagreement and compromise rather than one student deciding everything. Strong paragraphs say whose idea each part of the plot came from.

quests.title: What If Dominoes
quests.text: Gather at least four classmates near the fountain and start a "what if" chain in nearby chat: "If the fountain granted wishes, everyone would want to visit Pixel Plaza." The next person turns your result into a new "if": "If everyone wanted to visit Pixel Plaza, the hotel would be full." Keep the dominoes falling until everyone has added a link. Useful phrases: "If that happened, ...", "That would mean ...". Write a short paragraph retelling the chain and saying which consequence was the most surprising or the most logical, and why.
quests.teacherNote: Check that each new "if" clause changes the previous "would + verb" into the past simple (would be full becomes If the hotel were full). With a big class, run two chains at once and compare where they end.

quests.title: The Great Cake Disaster
quests.text: Role-play with a classmate. Yesterday there was a Great Cake Disaster at the cafe: a giant chocolate cake ended up on the floor. One of you is the waiter, the other is the customer, and each of you is sure the other is to blame. Tell your versions in detail, question each other, then negotiate an "official version" you can both accept. Useful phrases: "That's not exactly how it happened", "I admit that ..., but ...", "Let's agree that ...". Write a short paragraph summarising both versions and the official story.
quests.teacherNote: Look for narrative tenses (was carrying, had already put) and reporting language in the summary (He claimed that...). Strong pairs can invite a third classmate to act as a witness.

quests.title: Fix the Plot Hole
quests.text: Fix this plot hole with two or three classmates: "At 9 pm, the famous Golden Spoon vanished from a locked hotel room with a closed window. The receptionist saw nobody go in or out. At 10 pm, the spoon was found in the park pond." Each person suggests an explanation; the others ask questions and point out weaknesses. Useful phrases: "It might have been ...", "Someone must have ...", "That can't be right because ...". Write a short paragraph summarising the theories and saying which one your group finds most convincing, and why.
quests.teacherNote: Target past modals of deduction (must have, might have, can't have). There is no single right answer; reward theories that explain all the clues: the locked door, the closed window and the pond.

quests.title: Pitch Your Story
quests.text: Invent a one-sentence story opening set somewhere in Pixel Plaza: the more intriguing, the better. Pitch it to at least four classmates, one by one, and persuade each of them to add the next sentence. If someone isn't convinced, ask why and try a different argument. Useful phrases: "Imagine if ...", "What makes this special is ...", "You'd be perfect for this because ...". Write a short paragraph: your opening, the sentences your classmates added, and which arguments worked best and why.
quests.teacherNote: Watch for persuasive language and polite responses to a "no"; nobody has to join. The paragraph should reflect on which arguments worked and why.

quests.title: Mystery Animal Whisper
quests.text: Think of an animal. Whisper clues to a classmate: "It is ... It has ... It lives in ..." They guess, then swap. Write: "My animal is a ... My classmate needs ... clues."
quests.teacherNote: Check is/has/lives and that nobody types the animal's name in a clue. For a challenge, ban the words big and small.

quests.title: Spot That Avatar
quests.text: Choose an avatar near you. Describe it in nearby chat: "This person has a ... shirt and ... hair." Be kind! Classmates guess the name. Write: "The avatar is ... and ... guesses first."
quests.teacherNote: Students describe avatars only (shirt, hat, hair colour, glasses), never real people's looks. Step in if a comment is unkind. Stronger students can add hats and glasses to the frame.

quests.title: Sleepy Place Riddle
quests.text: Read the clues: "You sleep here. You get a key at the desk. It has a lot of rooms." Ask a classmate: "Is it the ...?" Write the place in Pixel Plaza.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: the hotel (you sleep there, you get a key at the desk, it has many rooms). Fast finishers can write a three-clue riddle about the cafe or the shop and whisper it to a classmate.

quests.title: I Spy in the Plaza
quests.text: Choose a thing in Pixel Plaza. Tell 2-3 classmates: "I spy with my little eye something ..." (a colour). They ask: "Is it the ...?" Take turns. Write: "... guesses my thing: the ..."
quests.teacherNote: Good targets are the fountain, the bridge, a bench, a tree or the cafe sign. Ask for full questions ("Is it the fountain?"). For a harder version, play "something beginning with B".

quests.title: Noisy Clues
quests.text: Think of a thing that makes a noise. No animals! Whisper a sound clue to a classmate: "It goes beep beep!" They guess, then swap. Write: "My sound is ... It is a ..."
quests.teacherNote: Typical answers: tick tock (a clock), ring ring (a phone or a bell), vroom (a motorbike), beep beep (a car or a microwave). If a sound fits two things, let the guesser ask one yes/no question.

quests.title: Hotel Job Riddle
quests.text: Read and guess the job: "Yesterday I arrived at the hotel. A person at the front desk smiled, checked my name on the computer and gave me a room key." Whisper your idea to a classmate. Do they agree? Write the name of the job.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: receptionist (front desk, checks your name, gives you the key). The checker also accepts desk clerk, hotel clerk and concierge, plus the common spelling mistake recepcionist, so ask students to spell receptionist aloud afterwards.

quests.title: Ten Questions Challenge
quests.text: Ask a classmate to choose a secret thing you can buy in a shop. Guess it with only yes/no questions, for example: "Can you eat it?" "Is it bigger than a book?" You have 10 questions. Then swap. Write 2-3 sentences: what the thing was and which question helped most.
quests.teacherNote: Look for correct question forms (Is it...? Can you...? Do you...?). To make it harder, allow 5 questions. To make it easier, allow one wh- question.

quests.title: Guess My Day Out
quests.text: Imagine a day out (real or invented). Tell 2-3 classmates what you did, but don't say the place: "I went by bus. I saw lots of animals. I ate an ice cream." They ask: "Did you go to the ...?" Write 2-3 sentences: your clues and who guessed.
quests.teacherNote: Check regular and irregular past forms (went, saw, ate, bought). Invented days out are fine, so nobody has to share real plans. Good places: the beach, a museum, the cinema, a stadium, the mountains.

quests.title: Packing Puzzle
quests.text: Imagine a trip. Tell classmates in nearby chat what you are going to take: "I'm going to take a towel, sunglasses and a bucket." They guess: "Are you going to the ...?" Be creative: space is OK! Try it with 4 classmates. Write 2-3 sentences: your list and who guessed.
quests.teacherNote: Look for going to + verb in both the clues and the questions. Funny places like space, the North Pole or a desert island make the guessing more fun. The example in the text is the beach.

quests.title: Character Countdown
quests.text: Think of a famous cartoon or film character. Give 2-3 classmates one clue at a time, starting with a hard clue: "He wears a red hat." Count the clues. Useful phrases: "This character is...", "He/She can...", "Is it...?" Write 2-3 sentences: your character and how many clues they needed.
quests.teacherNote: Well-known options: SpongeBob, Shrek, Elsa, Mario, Pikachu. Clues should go from hard to easy, and the name never counts as a clue.

quests.title: Taboo Showdown
quests.text: Play Taboo with 2-3 classmates in nearby chat. Take turns: describe one card without using the word or its two forbidden words. Cards: PIZZA (cheese, Italy), HOLIDAY (summer, school), PHONE (call, mobile), FOOTBALL (ball, goal), DENTIST (teeth, doctor). Useful phrases: "It's something you...", "It's a kind of...", "You need it when..." Write 3-5 sentences: which card was hardest, which clue worked best, and why.
quests.teacherNote: You can check the chat log for forbidden words afterwards. Groups that finish early can make their own cards and swap them with another group.

quests.title: Cities Without Houses
quests.text: Solve this riddle: "I have cities, but no houses. I have forests, but no trees. I have rivers, but no water. Hikers unfold me when they are lost." Before you answer, whisper the riddle to a classmate and compare ideas. Useful phrases: "I think it's... because...", "It can't be... because..." Type your answer in one or two words.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: a map (an atlas is also accepted). It has cities, forests and rivers that are only drawn, and hikers unfold it. Listen for reasoning such as "It can't be a forest because...".

quests.title: The Job Hot Seat
quests.text: Choose a secret job (not one in Pixel Plaza). Stand in the square and invite at least 4 classmates to ask you questions in nearby chat: "Do you work outside?" "Do you need special clothes?" Follow-up questions are great: "What do you use at work?" Answer truthfully and add details. Useful phrases: "Not really, but...", "Sometimes, especially when..." When someone guesses, ask: "Would you like this job? Why?" Write 3-5 sentences: the best questions, who guessed, and their opinion.
quests.teacherNote: Encourage open follow-up questions after the yes/no ones. Fun jobs to suggest: firefighter, vet, astronaut, lifeguard, chef, zookeeper.

quests.title: Comparatives Only
quests.text: Think of an animal or a vehicle. Your partner must guess it, but you can only give clues with comparatives: "It's bigger than a cat but smaller than a horse." "It's faster than a bike." Your partner can ask: "Is it more dangerous than a dog?" Swap roles. Useful phrases: "It's much heavier than...", "It isn't as fast as..." Write 3-5 sentences: your best comparison clues and how many your partner needed.
quests.teacherNote: Check comparative forms (heavier, more dangerous, not as fast as). For a challenge, ban big and small so students need words like longer, louder or more expensive.

quests.title: Postcard From Somewhere
quests.text: Imagine you are visiting a famous place in the world: a city, a monument or a natural wonder. Play with at least 4 classmates. Send postcard clues in nearby chat without saying its name: "It's rainier than here and there's a famous clock tower." When someone guesses, ask: "Would you like to visit it? Why or why not?" Useful phrases: "I'd love to go because...", "It sounds..., but..." Write 3-5 sentences: your place, your best clue and two classmates' opinions.
quests.teacherNote: Good places: Paris, New York, Venice, the Sahara, Mount Everest, the Great Wall of China (the example is London). Ask for reasons in the opinions, not just yes or no.

quests.title: What-If Detectives
quests.text: Play with 2-3 classmates. Secretly choose a famous fictional character. The others can only ask hypothetical questions: "If this character were an animal, what would they be?" "If they came to Pixel Plaza, where would they go first?" Answer creatively but fairly. The group may make only one guess per round, so they must discuss and agree first. Take turns. Useful phrases: "If they were..., they'd...", "I reckon it might be... since..." Write a short paragraph summarising which questions were most revealing, how your group agreed on guesses, and where you disagreed.
quests.teacherNote: Look for second conditional forms and for discussion before each guess. Well-known characters work best: Harry Potter, Elsa, Shrek, Sherlock Holmes, Mario.

quests.title: Taboo Card Makers
quests.text: Design two Taboo cards with a partner: a target word and three forbidden words for each. Negotiate: the cards must be hard but fair, so discuss which forbidden words to choose. Then test each card on a different classmate outside your pair by describing it in nearby chat or a whisper. Useful phrases: "What if we banned...?", "That's too harsh, because...", "Fair enough, but..." Write a short paragraph: your cards, what you disagreed about and how you decided, and whether the test proved you right.
quests.teacherNote: Strong pairs explain their choices ("If we ban water, they'll have to talk about..."). Collect the best cards for a whole-class Taboo round later.

quests.title: Invention Pitch
quests.text: Choose an ordinary object and present it in nearby chat as an amazing new invention, without naming it: "Tired of wet hair on rainy days? This light, foldable device..." Classmates must guess the object. Then answer their doubts and try to convince at least 4 of them that they can't live without it. Useful phrases: "Imagine never having to...", "Unlike other products, this...", "I see your point, but..." Write a short paragraph: your pitch, the doubts people raised, how you answered them, and how many classmates you convinced.
quests.teacherNote: Look for persuasive structures and polite counter-arguments. Funny everyday choices (a spoon, a sock, a stapler) make the best pitches. The example in the text is an umbrella.

quests.title: Alien Field Report
quests.text: Imagine you are an alien scientist studying humans in Pixel Plaza. Write three strange but accurate descriptions of human objects or habits without naming them, for example: "Every morning, humans pour white liquid from a large animal onto small dry pieces, then eat them with a metal tool." Post them one at a time in nearby chat and see who can decode them. Avoid obvious key words. Useful phrases: "a device that...", "a ritual in which..."
