Write a short paragraph: your descriptions, what classmates guessed, and which one was hardest to decode and why.
quests.teacherNote: The example is breakfast cereal with milk. Reward precise, funny paraphrasing (a phone is "a glowing rectangle humans stare at") and check that the key words are avoided.

quests.title: Explain the Invisible
quests.text: Take turns with 2-3 classmates: describe something you cannot see or touch, without naming it (a natural force, a sound, a technology or an idea). The others guess. Do at least two rounds each. Then rank the things from hardest to easiest to describe and agree on one group ranking. Useful phrases: "It's tricky to describe because...", "I'd put... above... since...", "Let's compromise:..." Write a short paragraph: your ranking, the different views in your group and how you reached agreement.
quests.teacherNote: If a group gets stuck, suggest wind, Wi-Fi, time, gravity, an echo or a secret. Listen for rankings with reasons and for compromise language.

quests.title: Operation Pizza
quests.text: Make a classmate type the secret word "pizza". You cannot type it first! Ask food questions, like "What food do you like?" Then write: "... says pizza when I ask about ..."
quests.teacherNote: Check that the student asked real questions (What do you eat on Fridays? What food is from Italy?) and did not just tell the classmate to type the word. If pizza is too hard, let them choose another food word.

quests.title: Colour Twin Hunt
quests.text: Find your colour twin! Ask four or more classmates: "What is your favourite colour?" Find someone with the same favourite colour as you. Write: "My favourite colour is ... and ... likes it too."
quests.teacherNote: If nobody has the same colour, the student can write the closest match (light blue and dark blue). Encourage students to answer everyone who asks them, so the whole class practises.

quests.title: Bridge Code Guards
quests.text: Choose an English code word with two classmates. Stand on the bridge. Ask everyone: "Can you guess our code word?" Give clues: "It is green." Write: "Our code word is ... and ... guesses it."
quests.teacherNote: Look for short clue sentences like "It is big" or "It can fly". If nobody guesses, the student writes "nobody guesses it", and the mission still counts as done.

quests.title: Crack the Number Code
quests.text: Crack the code: A=1, B=2, C=3 and so on. The secret agent's favourite food is 3-1-11-5. Type the food. Then whisper your own code to a classmate, like: "Can you read 4-15-7?"
quests.teacherNote: Solution: 3-1-11-5 is C-A-K-E, so the answer is cake. Fast finishers can swap number codes with classmates (4-15-7 is dog).

quests.title: Agent Name Maker
quests.text: Give a classmate an agent name from their avatar, like "Agent Red Hat". Whisper it and ask: "Do you like it?" They name you too. Write: "I am Agent ... and ... is Agent ..."
quests.teacherNote: Names must be friendly and based only on the avatar's colours and clothes (hat, glasses, shirt, hair colour). If a classmate does not like their name, they choose a new one together.

quests.title: Season Detective
quests.text: Find out a classmate's favourite season, but don't ask "What's your favourite season?" Ask about weather, clothes and holidays. Useful phrases: "Do you like hot weather?", "What do you do in winter?" At the end, check your guess. Write 2-3 sentences: what you asked, your guess and if you were right.
quests.teacherNote: Look for indirect questions about weather, clothes and activities, and past simple in the report. Extension: the partner then guesses the student's favourite season the same way.

quests.title: Word Smuggler
quests.text: Chat with two or three classmates in nearby chat. Secretly use these words in normal sentences: umbrella, dinosaur, sandwich. Example: "I saw a dinosaur film last week." Then ask: "Can you guess my three secret words?" Write 2-3 sentences: how you used them and who guessed.
quests.teacherNote: Praise sentences that fit naturally into the conversation, because hiding the words is the real challenge. You can swap the three words for vocabulary from the current story chapter.

quests.title: Secret Meeting Plan
quests.text: Plan a secret meeting with a classmate. Where and when are you going to meet? Invent a code question and answer, like "Is the cafe open?" - "Only for ducks." Then meet there and test it! Useful phrases: "Let's meet at...", "We're going to..." Write 3 sentences about your plan.
quests.teacherNote: Check for "going to" and suggestions (Let's..., How about...?). Encourage the pair to really meet at the place and try their code question and answer.

quests.title: Undercover Object
quests.text: Choose a secret thing in Pixel Plaza, like a bench, a cup of coffee or a duck. Tell four classmates: "I'm a secret thing. Ask me yes/no questions!" Useful questions: "Are you in the park?", "Can people eat you?" Write 2-3 sentences: what you chose, who guessed and how many questions they asked.
quests.teacherNote: Check question forms (Are you...? Can you...? Is it...?). Students can choose a new secret thing for each classmate to keep the game fresh.

quests.title: First Letter Secret
quests.text: Read the secret message: "Funny Old Uncles Never Tell Anyone Interesting News." The first letters of the words spell the meeting place. Type the place. Then hide a word in a sentence like this and whisper it to a classmate. Can they find it?
quests.teacherNote: Solution: the first letters spell F-O-U-N-T-A-I-N, so the answer is fountain. Writing their own hidden-word sentences is good extra vocabulary practice.

quests.title: Spot the Double Agent
quests.text: Tell your group three facts about yourself: two true, one a lie. Choose safe topics like hobbies, food or places you have visited. The group asks follow-up questions to find the lie, and you defend it. Then swap roles. Useful phrases: "When did you...?", "I think it's a lie because..." Write 3-5 sentences: your facts, the best questions and who found your lie.
quests.teacherNote: Remind students to use facts about themselves only and nothing private (no addresses, family problems, etc.). Look for follow-up questions in the past simple and present perfect.

quests.title: Common Ground Mission
quests.text: Find something surprising you have in common with four different classmates, ideally people you don't often talk to. Obvious things like "We both like pizza" don't count! Ask follow-up questions to go deeper. Useful phrases: "Me too! What about...?", "Have you ever...?", "Really? Which one?" Write 3-5 sentences: who you talked to and what you have in common.
quests.teacherNote: Strong answers go beyond food and colours (both collect something, both can't whistle, both have been to the same beach). Watch that nobody is left out, and pair up students who are still looking.

quests.title: Gadget Lab
quests.text: Invent a helpful spy gadget made from an everyday object, like a pen or an umbrella. Describe it to a classmate without naming the object: can they guess it? Then ask about their gadget and decide together which one is more useful and why. Useful phrases: "It's used for...", "It can...", "... is more useful than... because..." Write 3-5 sentences about both gadgets and your decision.
quests.teacherNote: Look for "is used for" and comparatives with reasons. Keep gadgets helpful and harmless (no weapons).

quests.title: Who Has the Key
quests.text: Solve the mystery: four agents are at the cafe, but only one has the secret key. Agent Owl is the youngest. Agent Bear is older than Agent Fox. Agent Cat is younger than Agent Fox. The agent with the key is older than Agent Cat but isn't the oldest. Who has the key? Type the agent's name. Then explain your reasoning to a classmate. Useful phrases: "It can't be... because...", "So it must be..."
quests.teacherNote: Solution: from youngest to oldest the order is Owl, Cat, Fox, Bear, so the agent who is older than Cat but not the oldest is Fox. Ask students to justify it, e.g. "It can't be Bear because Bear is the oldest".

quests.title: Pass It On, Agent
quests.text: Start a top-secret relay with two or three classmates and explain the rules first. Whisper this message to the first agent: "The golden duck will meet you near the fountain after lunch, so bring a sandwich." Each agent passes it on in their own words, without copying. The last agent whispers it back to you. Useful phrases: "In other words...", "It means that..." Write 3-5 sentences: how the message changed and which version you prefer.
quests.teacherNote: Good paraphrases keep the meaning but change the words ("after lunch" becomes "in the afternoon"). For weaker groups, let each agent change only two or three words.

quests.title: Operation It Depends
quests.text: Make classmates say "it depends" without ever saying it yourself. Ask open questions with no simple answer, for example "Is it better to live in a city or a village?" When someone says it, ask a follow-up: "On what?" Try with at least four classmates, and no cheating like "Please say it depends!" Write a short paragraph: which questions worked, what the answers depended on, and why you think those questions worked.
quests.teacherNote: Strong strategies use dilemmas and comparisons (Which is better...? Should...?). Look for nuanced answers after "On what?", such as "It depends on how much free time you have".

quests.title: Undercover Opinion Poll
quests.text: Find out what four classmates think about this question without asking it directly: "Should school start an hour later?" Instead, chat about mornings, sleep, after-school activities and free time, and guess each person's opinion. At the end, reveal your mission and check whether you were right. Useful phrases: "How do you feel about...?", "Would you rather...?" Write a short paragraph summarising the different views, including any "yes, but..." answers, and how accurate your guesses were.
quests.teacherNote: Look for summarising language (Most people..., While X thinks..., Y was less sure because...). You can swap the topic for any current class debate, such as homework at weekends.

quests.title: The Golden Duck Alibi
quests.text: Investigate the case of the missing golden duck statue, which vanished from the fountain yesterday between 4 and 5 pm. In a group of three, two classmates are the suspects: give them two minutes to invent a detailed alibi together (where they were and what they did). You are the detective. Whisper questions to each suspect separately, such as "What exactly did you order?" or "What was the weather like?", and compare their answers. Any difference proves they're guilty! Write a short paragraph explaining which details matched, which didn't, and your final verdict.
quests.teacherNote: Look for past continuous and past simple (What were you doing at 4.30? What did you order?) and precise follow-up questions. Rotate roles so everyone gets to be the detective, and keep the tone playful.

quests.title: Spy Dilemma Debate
quests.text: Discuss three spy dilemmas with a classmate and try to agree on the best plan for each. One: what would you do if you found a secret map under a park bench? Two: if your code phrase were discovered, how would you warn your team? Three: would you rather have an invisibility gadget or a flying one, and why? Useful phrases: "If I were you, I'd...", "That might work, but..." Write a short paragraph summarising both opinions and what you agreed on.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for the second conditional and polite disagreement. Pairs who finish early can invent a fourth dilemma for another pair.

quests.title: Secret HQ Showdown
quests.text: Choose the perfect secret headquarters for your spy team. With two or three classmates, each agent argues for a different place in Pixel Plaza: the hotel, the cafe, the shop or the park. Give convincing reasons (hidden corners, a good view, easy escape, snacks) and answer the others' arguments. You must reach one decision together, so be ready to compromise. Useful phrases: "I see your point, but...", "What if we...?", "Wouldn't it be better to...?" Write a short paragraph summarising each agent's argument, the final decision and why it won.
quests.teacherNote: Look for persuasive language and real compromise (the cafe by day, the park at night). If the group agrees too quickly, ask each student to argue for a place they did not pick first.

quests.title: Our Class Pet
quests.text: Choose a class pet with a classmate: a cat, a fish, a rabbit or a hamster. Ask: "Do you like cats?" Agree on one pet. Write: "Our class pet is a ... because ..."
quests.teacherNote: Check in the chat log that the pair asked at least one question before agreeing. For a challenge, ask them to add a name for the pet.

quests.title: Party Place Vote
quests.text: Ask 4 classmates: "What is the best place for a class party: the cafe, the park or the hotel?" Count the votes. Write: "The winner is the ... with ... votes."
quests.teacherNote: Students can stand in the square and ask in nearby chat. If there is a tie, they can ask one more classmate or write "It is a draw."

quests.title: Island Bag
quests.text: Imagine you are on an island with 2 or 3 classmates. Choose 2 things together: water, a hat, a ball, a torch or a book. Write: "We take ... and ... because ..."
quests.teacherNote: Any choice is fine; the point is that the group talks before deciding. Faster groups can add which thing they leave behind and why (pre-teach "torch" if needed).

quests.title: Picnic by the Pond
quests.text: Meet a classmate at the pond and plan a picnic. Say "I like ..." or "I don't like ...". Choose 3 foods together. Write: "We take ..., ... and ... to the picnic."
quests.teacherNote: Look for "I like / I don't like" in the chat before the decision. Stronger students can add one drink and one game for the picnic.

quests.title: The Oldest Invention
quests.text: Guess the oldest invention: the phone, the wheel or the computer. Ask a classmate: "What do you think?" Then type the oldest one.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: the wheel (about 5,500 years old); the phone is from the 1870s and the computer from the 20th century. Extend it by asking students to rank all three in the chat.

quests.title: Class Trip Plan
quests.text: Plan a class trip with 2 or 3 classmates. Choose a place (the beach, the mountains, a theme park or a big city) and one activity. Useful phrases: "Let's go to ...", "What about ...?", "Good idea!" Write 3 sentences: where you are going to go, what you are going to do and why.
quests.teacherNote: Check that the sentences use "going to". If the group cannot agree, they can vote and mention the vote in their answer.

quests.title: Mascot Election
quests.text: Find a mascot for your class. Suggest an animal in nearby chat. Then ask 4 classmates: "Which mascot do you vote for?" Useful phrases: "I vote for the ...", "It's cute/funny/strong." Write 3 sentences: which animals people suggested, how many votes each one got and which one won.
quests.teacherNote: If several students run this quest at the same time, the vote gets livelier. Look for past simple forms (suggested, got, won) in the answers.

quests.title: Lunch Menu Ranking
quests.text: Rank these school lunches from 1 (best) to 5 (worst): pasta, fish, salad, pizza, soup. Compare with a classmate and make one list together. Useful phrases: "My number one is ...", "I agree.", "I don't agree because ..." Write 3 sentences: your number one, your number five and one thing you disagreed about.
quests.teacherNote: Pairs should agree on one shared list, not just report two separate lists. You can swap the foods for local favourites.

quests.title: Sports Day Vote
quests.text: Read the clues. Your class voted for one sport for sports day. Basketball got more votes than tennis. Volleyball got fewer votes than tennis. Football got the most votes. Which sport came last? Check with a classmate, then type the sport.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: volleyball (order: football, basketball, tennis, volleyball). Early finishers can write their own vote puzzle and whisper it to a classmate.

quests.title: Class Superpower
quests.text: Agree on ONE superpower for your whole class with a classmate: flying, being invisible, speaking every language or stopping time. Useful phrases: "I think ... is better because ...", "OK, let's choose ..." Write 3 sentences: your choice, one reason, and one thing the class is going to do with it.
quests.teacherNote: Encourage pairs to compare the options ("better than", "more useful than") before deciding. Funny ideas are welcome as long as they are kind.

quests.title: Invention Top Three
quests.text: Rank these inventions from most to least important: the wheel, the fridge, the bicycle, the internet, the toothbrush. Then compare your list with a classmate and agree on a shared top three. Ask follow-up questions, e.g. "Why is that more important than the bicycle?" Useful phrases: "I'd put ... first because ...", "... is more useful than ...", "Fair point, but ..." Write 4 sentences: your shared top three, the best reason you heard and one thing you disagreed about.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for comparatives and real reasons, not just a list. To reuse it, swap in other inventions (the phone, glasses, the washing machine).

quests.title: Desert Island Survival
quests.text: Imagine your boat is stuck on a desert island for one week. You can keep only 4 of these: a rope, a mirror, a tent, matches, sunscreen, a fishing net, a guitar, a cooking pot. Discuss with 2 or 3 classmates and agree on your 4. Useful phrases: "We need ... because ...", "... is more useful than ...", "What if it rains?" Write 4-5 sentences: your 4 items, why you chose them and one item you were sad to leave.
quests.teacherNote: There is no single right answer; good groups explain how they would use each item (the mirror for signalling, the pot for boiling water). If there is time, groups can compare lists with another group.

quests.title: Plaza Upgrade
quests.text: Find out what your town needs. Pixel Plaza can build ONE new place: a skate park, a cinema, a swimming pool or a library. Ask at least 4 classmates which one they prefer and why. Ask a follow-up question, e.g. "How often would you go there?" Useful phrases: "Which would you prefer?", "Most people think ...", "Only one person ..." Write 4-5 sentences: the most popular choice, the best reason you heard and your own opinion.
quests.teacherNote: Look for reported results ("Three people prefer...") and a personal opinion with a reason. You can change the four options to match a unit topic.

quests.title: New Class Rule
quests.text: Agree on ONE new fun rule for your class with 2 or 3 classmates. Everyone suggests one idea, for example music while you work, a joke every Friday, or a five-minute break after a test. Compare the ideas and choose the best one. Useful phrases: "That would be fun, but ...", "I prefer ... because ...", "Shall we vote?" Write 4 sentences: everyone's ideas, the winner and why you chose it.
quests.teacherNote: The rule should be kind and realistic; you could even try the winning rule for a week. Listen for "would" and comparisons while they choose.

quests.title: Mascot Ranking Puzzle
quests.text: Solve the puzzle. A class ranked five mascot ideas from 1st to 5th: a fox, an owl, a dragon, a penguin and a robot. The robot came first. The fox came last. The owl came one place before the penguin. The dragon did not come second. Which mascot came third? Compare your answer with a classmate, then type it.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: penguin (order: robot, owl, penguin, dragon, fox). The key clue is that the dragon cannot be second, so the owl must be second and the penguin third.

quests.title: Balloon Debate
quests.text: Imagine your hot-air balloon is sinking and it carries four great inventions: electricity, the printing press, the internet and the fridge. Each person defends one invention (in a group of three, drop one first). Take turns explaining why the world would be worse without yours. Then negotiate which invention goes overboard first, then second, until only one is left. Useful phrases: "Without ..., we wouldn't be able to ...", "I see your point, but ...", "If we lost ..., ..." Write a short paragraph: which invention survived, the strongest argument you heard and whether anyone changed your mind.
quests.teacherNote: Look for conditional arguments ("If we didn't have...") and polite disagreement. Students throw out inventions only, never people or avatars.

quests.title: Trip on a Budget
quests.text: Plan a three-day class trip with a classmate. You have 100 points (not real money). Transport: train 30 or bus 15. Sleeping: hotel 50, youth hostel 30 or camping 10. Activities: theme park 40, kayaking 25, cooking class 20, museum 10. Negotiate so that each of you gets at least one thing you really want. Useful phrases: "If we take the bus, we could afford ...", "I'd accept ... as long as ...", "How about a compromise?" Write a short paragraph: your final plan, what each of you gave up and why it is fair.
quests.teacherNote: Check that the plan costs 100 points or less and that the paragraph explains the compromise, not just the choices. Change the prices to make it harder.

quests.title: Party Theme Summit
quests.text: Help your class choose a theme for an end-of-term party (or another celebration you like): 80s disco, video games, beach party or superheroes. Talk to at least 5 classmates, ask which theme they prefer and what would make it fun for everyone. Note where people agree and disagree. Then propose a compromise that keeps most people happy, such as mixing two themes. Useful phrases: "Most people seem to ...", "On the other hand, ...", "What if we combined ...?" Write a short paragraph summarising the different views and your final proposal.
quests.teacherNote: A strong answer reports several views ("Some people..., while others...") before making a proposal. If a real class event is coming up, use it instead.

quests.title: Museum of Today
quests.text: Imagine a museum in 100 years wants three everyday objects to show how teenagers live today. With 2 or 3 classmates, suggest objects, then negotiate a final list of three. For each one, agree on what it would tell future visitors about life today. Useful phrases: "People in the future might think ...", "That says a lot about ...", "I'd swap ... for ... because ..." Write a short paragraph: your three objects, what each one shows and one object you argued about.
quests.teacherNote: Push for reasons beyond "it's popular": what the object shows about habits, values or technology. It works well before a unit on the past or the future.

quests.title: Robot Helper Deal
quests.text: Imagine your school gets one robot, but it can only do three jobs: clean the classrooms, serve lunch, carry heavy bags, help with homework, translate for new students or organise the library. Choose your three alone first, then negotiate one shared list with a classmate. Discuss the downsides too: "If the robot helped with homework, would we learn less?" Useful phrases: "The main advantage is ...", "The problem with that is ...", "Fair enough, I'll give up ... if ..." Write a short paragraph: your final three jobs, why, and one disadvantage you discussed.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for second conditionals and arguments that weigh both sides. Fast pairs can rank all six jobs.

quests.title: Dream Job Hunt
quests.text: Ask 4 classmates in nearby chat: "What is your dream job?" Answer their question too. Then write 2 sentences: "My dream job is ... ." and "(name) wants to be ... ."
quests.teacherNote: Check a/an with jobs (a vet, an astronaut) and the -s in "wants". For an extra challenge, ask students to find someone with the same dream job as them.

quests.title: Pick Your Superpower
quests.text: Whisper to a classmate: "Do you want to fly, be invisible or talk to animals?" Say your choice too. Write: "I want to ... because ... . My partner wants to ... ."
quests.teacherNote: Look for "wants" with -s for the partner and a simple reason after "because". Fast pairs can invent a fourth superpower and ask another classmate.

quests.title: Space Job Scramble
quests.text: Put the letters in order to find a dream job: T-U-A-N-O-R-T-S-A. Clue: this person works in space. Ask a classmate: "Do you want this job?" Type the job.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: ASTRONAUT (the 9 letters T-U-A-N-O-R-T-S-A make only this word). Fast finishers can make a scrambled job for a classmate to solve in the chat.

quests.title: Robot Helper Team
quests.text: Invent a robot helper for Pixel Plaza with 2 or 3 classmates. Each person says one thing it does in nearby chat. Then write: "Our robot is called ... . It ... and it ... ."
quests.teacherNote: Check the -s on verbs after "it" (it cleans, it makes, it carries). Groups can post their robot's name in the chat so the class can vote for a favourite.

quests.title: Fountain Wishes
quests.text: Go to the fountain in the square with a classmate. Each of you makes a wish in nearby chat: "I wish for ... ." Then write: "My wish is ... . My partner wishes for ... ."
quests.teacherNote: Encourage fun, imaginative wishes (a pet dragon, a pizza tree) rather than personal ones. Check "wishes" with -es for the partner.

quests.title: Weekend Plans Match
quests.text: Ask classmates in nearby chat: "What are you going to do this weekend?" Find 2 people with a plan like yours (or a plan you like). Useful phrases: "I'm going to ...", "Me too!", "Really? That sounds fun!" Write 3 sentences about your plan and the 2 people you found.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for "I'm going to + verb" and the correct question form. Remind students that "relax at home" is a perfectly good plan, so nobody feels left out.

quests.title: Pixel Plaza 2050
quests.text: Imagine Pixel Plaza in the year 2050 with 2 or 3 classmates. Decide together what is going to be different at the hotel, the cafe and the park. Useful phrases: "The cafe is going to have ...", "There are going to be ...". Write 3 sentences, one for each place.
quests.teacherNote: Check "there are going to be" + plural nouns. Groups can walk to each place and post their idea there in nearby chat.

quests.title: Bolt's Big Birthday
quests.text: Read: "Bolt the robot was built in 2026. In 2050, Bolt is going to have a big birthday party." How old is Bolt going to be at the party? Check your answer with a classmate. Type the number.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: 24 (2050 minus 2026). Fast finishers can write their own robot birthday puzzle for a classmate in the chat.

quests.title: Last Year, Next Year
quests.text: Whisper to a classmate. Ask: "What new thing did you learn last year?" and "What new thing are you going to try next year?" Ask "Why?" too. Then answer their questions. Useful phrases: "Last year I learned to ...", "Next year I'm going to try ...". Write 3 sentences about your partner.
quests.teacherNote: Look for correct past forms (learned/learnt, did you learn) and "going to + verb"; partners should report in third person ("She learned to ...").

quests.title: Fortune Cafe
quests.text: Go to the cafe and be a fortune teller! Give 4 classmates a kind, funny prediction in nearby chat: "Next week you are going to ...". Ask for a prediction too. Write 3 sentences: two predictions you gave and your favourite one you got.
quests.teacherNote: Predictions must be kind and silly ("you are going to find a lost sock"), never about looks or anything personal; moderate the chat for unkind messages. Check "you are going to + verb".

quests.title: Moon Base or Sea Base
quests.text: Ask at least 4 classmates in nearby chat: "In 2050, would you rather live in a city on the Moon or under the sea?" Ask a follow-up question each time, like "What would you miss most?" Keep count of the answers. Useful phrases: "I'd rather ... because ...", "That's a good point, but ...". Write 4 sentences: the results, the most interesting reason you heard, and your own choice with a reason.
quests.teacherNote: Check "I'd rather + base verb" (not "I'd rather to live"). Results can be given as "3 out of 5 people ...", a good chance to practise comparisons.

quests.title: Dream Job Detective
quests.text: Solve this puzzle. Mia, Leo and Sara each want a different dream job: chef, pilot or vet. Leo is afraid of flying. Sara is allergic to cats and dogs. Mia wants to work with animals. Who wants to be the pilot? Explain your thinking to a classmate in nearby chat before you answer. Useful phrases: "It can't be ... because ...", "So ... must be the ...". Type only the name.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: Sara. Mia works with animals, so she is the vet; Leo is afraid of flying, so he is the chef; that leaves Sara as the pilot (her allergy confirms she cannot be the vet).

quests.title: Time Capsule Team
quests.text: Plan a time capsule for Pixel Plaza players in 2050 with 2 or 3 classmates. Each person suggests one object and explains why it shows life today. Discuss and agree on the best three. Useful phrases: "We should include ... because ...", "I think ... is more important than ...", "OK, let's choose ...". Write 4 sentences: the three objects your group chose and why, and one idea you didn't choose.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for suggestions and comparatives (more important than, better than). The objects are imaginary, so no real items are needed; a follow-up question could be "What will students in 2050 think of it?"

quests.title: Future Me Interview
quests.text: Interview a classmate by whisper about their life at age 25. Ask at least 4 questions with "will", for example "What job will you have?" or "Will you have a pet?" After each answer, ask a follow-up question. Then swap roles. Useful phrases: "I think I'll ...", "I probably won't ...", "Maybe I'll ...". Write 4 sentences about your partner's future life.
quests.teacherNote: Check "will + base verb" and adverb position ("I'll probably ...", "I probably won't ..."). Students should report in third person ("She thinks she'll be a vet") and keep to fun topics, not where people will live exactly.

quests.title: The If Chain
quests.text: Build an "if chain" in nearby chat with 2 or 3 classmates. Start: "If I find a time machine, I will go to 2050." The next person begins with the end of that sentence: "If I go to 2050, I will ..." Keep going for at least 8 sentences. Useful phrases: "If I ..., I will ...", "If that happens, ...". Write your 4 favourite sentences from the chain, in order.
quests.teacherNote: Check the first conditional pattern (if + present simple, will + verb); the typical error is "If I will go". The chain can be as silly as students like as long as it stays kind.

quests.title: Invention Prize Jury
quests.text: Hold the Pixel Plaza Invention Prize with 2 or 3 classmates. Each person pitches an invention that would make life in 2050 easier or more fun. After each pitch, the others ask tough questions, such as "What would happen if it broke?" or "Who would actually use it?" Then negotiate a winner; nobody can vote for their own idea. Useful phrases: "Imagine if ...", "The main advantage is ...", "I see your point, but ...". Write a short paragraph: summarise the inventions, explain which one won and why, and mention one doubt your group still has about it.
quests.teacherNote: Look for persuasive language and hypotheticals (it would save time, if it broke we could ...). To adapt, give each group a theme such as school, sport or the environment.

quests.title: Superpower Swap Meet
quests.text: Choose a starting superpower: reading minds, teleporting, talking to animals or stopping time. Then mingle in nearby chat and try to swap it for a better one. To get a swap, convince classmates that your power is more useful than theirs, but be honest about one downside if they ask. Make at least 3 offers. Useful phrases: "If you had my power, you could ...", "I'd swap, but only if ...", "Think about it: ...". Write a short paragraph: which power you started and finished with, which arguments worked best and why you think so.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for the second conditional (if you had ..., you could ...) and conditions (only if, as long as). The downsides students mention (e.g. hearing everyone's thoughts) make a good whole-class debrief.

quests.title: Robots at Work Debate
quests.text: Debate this statement with 3 classmates: "By 2050, robots will do most jobs, and that is a good thing." Two of you argue for it and two against, even if you disagree. After a few minutes, switch sides. Finally, drop your roles and try to find a view everyone can accept. Useful phrases: "On the one hand ...", "That might be true, but ...", "What worries me is ...". Write a short paragraph summarising the strongest argument on each side and your own honest opinion.
quests.teacherNote: Check that summaries represent both sides fairly and use hedging (might, could, probably). With a group of 3, the third person can be a judge who summarises both sides.

quests.title: Message from 2050
quests.text: Imagine you have just travelled back from the year 2050 and you can give today's teenagers only three pieces of advice. Decide what they are and how you would justify them. Post your best piece of advice in nearby chat and ask at least two classmates whether they would follow it and why. Useful phrases: "If I were you, I'd ...", "By 2050, ... will have ...", "You might regret it if ...". Write a short paragraph with your three pieces of advice, your reasons, and how your classmates reacted.
quests.teacherNote: Look for advice structures (If I were you, you should, you might regret) and the future perfect (will have + past participle). Fun advice about technology, school or the planet works well; steer away from personal topics.

quests.title: The Frog's Wish
focus: Conditions: as long as / only if
quests.text: Meet a classmate on the little bridge in the park. A magic frog from the pond offers you just one shared wish, but every wish comes with a catch. Take turns: one of you proposes a wish, the other invents a funny catch, for example "You can fly, but only at walking speed." Negotiate, changing the wording each time, until you find a wish you would both accept. Useful phrases: "That's fine as long as ...", "What if we changed it to ...?", "I'd only agree if ...". Write a short paragraph describing your best rejected wish, your final wish and how you reached an agreement.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for conditions (as long as, provided that, only if) and suggestions with "what if we ...". The catches should stay funny, not scary or mean.

quests.title: Where To Next?
quests.text: Ask four classmates in the chat: "Where do you want to go on holiday?" Then ask "Why?" Write 2 sentences: "... wants to go to ... because ..."
quests.teacherNote: Listen for the third-person -s in "wants" and simple because-clauses. For a challenge, ask students to find two classmates with the same dream place.

quests.title: Odd One Out
quests.text: Find the word that is not a country: Italy, Japan, Paris, Brazil, Canada. Write the answer: "... is not a country." Then whisper a new puzzle like this to a classmate.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: Paris, because it is a city and the other four are countries. Answers like "Paris is not a country" are accepted, and the whispered puzzles are a nice extra to read in the chat.

quests.title: ABC Suitcase
quests.text: Pack an ABC suitcase with a partner. Take turns: "I pack an apple." "I pack a book." "I pack a cap." How far can you go? Write your last 3 things: "We pack ..."
quests.teacherNote: Check a/an (an apple, an umbrella, a map). Tricky letters like Q, X and Z can be skipped, or students can invent funny items.

quests.title: World Cafe Menu
quests.text: Go to the cafe with 2 or 3 classmates. Each person names a food and its country: "Sushi is from Japan." Find 4 different foods. Write 2 sentences: "... is from ..."
quests.teacherNote: Expect pizza, pasta and sushi; praise less obvious ones (curry from India, crepes from France). If the chat blocks a dish name, students can describe it in English, e.g. "a rice dish from Spain".

quests.title: Where Am I?
quests.text: Play "Where am I?" with a partner. Think of a country. Give 2 clues: "It is very hot. I can see kangaroos." Your partner guesses. Then swap. Write your partner's clues and the answer.
quests.teacherNote: Good clues mention weather, animals, food or famous places. If guessing takes too long, allow a third clue.

quests.title: Holiday Memory Hunt
quests.text: Find a different classmate for each one: saw snow, swam in the sea, ate food from another country, visited a museum. Ask: "Did you see snow last year?" Useful phrases: "Yes, I did." "No, I didn't." Write 3 sentences: "... saw snow last year."
quests.teacherNote: Look for "Did you + base verb" in the questions and past forms (saw, swam, ate) in the journal. The items are everyday ones so nobody is left out; in small classes one classmate can cover two items.

quests.title: Pixel Hotel Check-In
quests.text: Meet a partner at the hotel. One person is the receptionist and one is a tourist with a funny pretend name. Useful phrases: "How many nights?" "Do you want breakfast?" "Here is your key." Then swap. Write 3 sentences about your tourist, for example: "Captain Pizza wants a room for 4 nights."
quests.teacherNote: Pretend names keep real personal data out; make sure nobody uses a classmate's name as a joke. Stronger pairs can add a problem, like no rooms with a view of the pond.

quests.title: Ski Bag Mistake
quests.text: Help Lucas pack for a ski trip. His bag has gloves, a scarf, a warm hat, ski boots, flip-flops and a coat. One thing is wrong! Check with a classmate: "I think the ... is wrong because ..." Write the wrong thing.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: the flip-flops, because a ski trip is cold and snowy. Spelling variants (flip flops, flipflops) and "sandals" are accepted.

quests.title: Postcard From Paradise
quests.text: Choose a dream holiday place with 2 or 3 classmates. Make a group postcard from there: take turns adding one sentence in the chat. Useful phrases: "Yesterday we visited ...", "We ate ...", "The weather was ...". Write your 3 favourite sentences in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Check past simple forms (visited, ate, saw, went). For extra fun, add a rule that every sentence must include one silly surprise.

quests.title: Lost Tourist Rescue
quests.text: Play "Lost Tourist" with a partner. The tourist starts at the hotel and asks: "Excuse me, how do I get to the bridge?" The guide whispers directions. Useful phrases: "Go past the fountain", "Turn left at the cafe". The tourist walks there. Then swap. Write your best directions in 2 or 3 sentences.
quests.teacherNote: On a top-down map, pairs may need to agree that left and right mean the screen's left and right. When they swap, the new tourist chooses a different place, such as the shop or the pond.

quests.title: The Travel Agent Game
quests.text: Work with a partner: one is a travel agent and one is a customer. The agent asks at least 5 questions (hot or cold? city or nature? favourite food?) and follow-up questions like "Why?" Then the agent recommends a destination and explains why it is perfect. Swap roles. Useful phrases: "What kind of ... do you prefer?", "I'd recommend ... because ...". Write 4 sentences: what your customer likes, where you sent them and why.
quests.teacherNote: Good answers link the customer's likes to the destination (loves snow and wildlife, so Canada or Norway). To stretch strong pairs, the customer can reject the first idea and ask for another.

quests.title: Four Tickets Puzzle
quests.text: Solve this puzzle with a classmate. Four friends have tickets to Tokyo, Cairo, Rome and Rio de Janeiro, one city each. Ben wants to see the pyramids. Ana is not going to Asia or South America. Dani wants to dance at a famous carnival near the beach. Where is Carla going? Useful phrases: "It can't be ... because ...", "So ... must be going to ...". Write the city.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: Tokyo. Ben goes to Cairo (pyramids) and Dani to Rio (carnival), so Ana, who is not going to Asia, gets Rome and Carla gets Tokyo.

quests.title: The Perfect Travel Buddy
quests.text: Find out what makes a perfect travel buddy. Ask at least 4 classmates: "Which is most important in a travel buddy: being funny, being organised or liking the same food?" Always ask a follow-up question, like "Why?" or "Can you give an example?" Useful phrases: "For me, the most important thing is ...", "I'd rather travel with someone who ...". Write 4 sentences: the most popular answer, one interesting reason, and your own opinion.
quests.teacherNote: Encourage real follow-up questions rather than just collecting votes. Change the three qualities (brave, calm, good with maps) to make a second round feel fresh.

quests.title: World Food Festival
quests.text: Plan a world food stall at the cafe with 2 or 3 classmates. Each person suggests one dish from a different country and describes it: what is in it, how it tastes and why people will love it. Ask each other questions, then choose the 2 best dishes for your stall. Useful phrases: "It's made with ...", "It tastes ...", "I think ... is better than ... because ...". Write 4 sentences about your 2 dishes and why they won.
quests.teacherNote: Push for describing words (spicy, sweet, crunchy, creamy) and comparatives. If the chat blocks a dish name, students can describe it in English instead (e.g. "a cold tomato soup from Spain").

quests.title: Travel Would You Rather
quests.text: Play "Would you rather" with 2 or 3 classmates. Take turns asking travel questions, for example: "Would you rather travel by train for two days or fly for twelve hours?" or "Would you rather visit a jungle or a desert?" Everyone answers and gives a reason. Useful phrases: "I'd rather ... because ...", "That's true, but ...". Write 4 sentences: your favourite question, what people chose and why.
quests.teacherNote: Students should invent their own questions after the two examples. Check "I'd rather + base verb" (not "I'd rather to").

quests.title: The Class Trip Showdown
quests.text: Imagine your class has won a free trip, but your group must choose the destination: a city break in London, a nature trip to Iceland, or five days at a theme park. Share out the options so each one has a defender, then persuade each other. Ask tough questions, point out weaknesses and negotiate until everyone accepts one choice or a clever compromise. Useful phrases: "Imagine how amazing it would be if ...", "I see your point, but ...", "What if we ...?" Write a short paragraph summarising the arguments for each option and how your group reached its final decision.
quests.teacherNote: Look for concession language (I see your point, but...; that may be true, however...). You can swap the three options for places your class is studying.

quests.title: The Backpack Dilemma
quests.text: Imagine you and a partner are backpacking around the world for a month and your bags are almost full. Between you, you can add only three more items (no phones or money). Each of you proposes three items and explains why they are essential. Then negotiate until you agree on a final three. Useful phrases: "Without a ..., we'd be in trouble if ...", "I could live without ... as long as ...", "Fair enough, but ...". Write a short paragraph explaining your final three items, what you gave up and why.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for conditionals (we'd be in trouble if it rained) and concession language. Reward creative items, like a deck of cards or a sewing kit, when the reasons are convincing.

quests.title: The Great Tourism Debate
quests.text: Interview at least 4 classmates about tourism in popular cities like Barcelona or Venice: "Is tourism good or bad for a busy city?" Use follow-ups like "Who benefits most?" or "What would you change if you were the mayor?" Try to find different points of view, and keep it respectful: talk about tourism, not nationalities. Useful phrases: "On the one hand ..., on the other hand ...", "It depends on ...", "Most people think ..., whereas ...". Write a short paragraph summarising the different views and giving your own balanced opinion.
quests.teacherNote: This topic is close to home in Catalonia, so steer students away from generalisations about nationalities. Strong paragraphs balance benefits (jobs, culture) and problems (crowds, noise, prices) before giving an opinion.

quests.title: Time Machine Tours
quests.text: Imagine you run a time-travel tour company. Invent one holiday to any city, past or future: ancient Rome, London in the 1960s, Tokyo in the year 3000. Go to the square and pitch your tour to at least 4 classmates: what they would see, eat and do, and why it is worth the risk. Listen to their pitches and ask tricky questions. Useful phrases: "If you came with us, you would ...", "Don't worry about ..., because ...", "I'd be tempted, but ...". Write a short paragraph: how many people you persuaded, the best pitch you heard and which tour you would choose and why.
quests.teacherNote: Keep destinations light-hearted and steer away from wars or disasters. Listen for second conditionals (If you came with us, you would...) and persuasive questions.

quests.title: Visit Pixel Plaza
quests.text: Persuade tourists to visit Pixel Plaza! Plan an advert that makes the hotel, the cafe, the shop, the fountain and the pond with its little bridge sound irresistible. Describe a perfect weekend here and include at least one conditional. Share your best line in the chat, ask two classmates if it would make them visit, then improve it. Useful phrases: "Imagine waking up to ...", "If you only visit one town this year, ...", "Whether you love ... or ..., ...". Write your final advert as a short paragraph.
quests.teacherNote: Reward vivid adjectives and persuasive techniques such as direct address, rhetorical questions and conditionals. A nice follow-up is to read two or three adverts aloud and let the class vote.

quests.title: Cafe Menu Mash-Up
quests.text: Ask a classmate: "What is your favourite food?" Make a new cafe dish with their food and your favourite food. Tell them! Write 1 sentence: "New at the cafe: ... with ...!"
quests.teacherNote: Expect funny mixes like "pizza with chocolate"; check food words and the preposition "with". Fast finishers can invent a name for the dish.

quests.title: Colour Poem Crew
quests.text: Ask three classmates: "What is your favourite colour?" Find a thing in Pixel Plaza for each colour. Write a 3-line poem and share it: "Red is the ... Blue is the ..."
quests.teacherNote: Accept anything students can see in the town (the pond, a hat, the cafe door). If a colour is hard to find, let them use any thing they know in that colour.

quests.title: Shop Slogan Shout
quests.text: Write a slogan for the shop: "Come to the shop! We have ... and ...!" Say it in nearby chat. Ask a classmate: "Do you like it?" Write your slogan and their answer.
quests.teacherNote: Check "We have" + plural nouns (hats, apples). Stronger students can add an adjective: "We have cool hats and big apples!"

quests.title: Postcard from the Pond
quests.text: Go to the park. Write a postcard to a classmate and whisper it: "Hi ...! I am in the park. I can see ... and ...!" Ask them to write back. Write your postcard.
quests.teacherNote: Students walk to the park first, so check they name things that are really there (the pond, the bridge, classmates' avatars). Partners can compare postcards afterwards.

quests.title: Birthday Card for the Fountain
quests.text: Make a birthday card for the fountain! Ask four classmates for a nice word, like "happy" or "sunny". Write your card: "Happy birthday, Fountain! Have a ..., ..., ... and ... day!"
quests.teacherNote: Check that students collect adjectives (not nouns) and use commas in the list. The card is for the fountain, not a real student, so nobody has to share their real birthday.

quests.title: The Duck's Diary
quests.text: Imagine you are a duck in the park pond. With a partner, write the duck's diary about yesterday. Take turns in whisper chat: you write one sentence, your partner writes the next. Useful phrases: "Dear Diary, yesterday I...", "Then I saw...", "In the evening...". Write your diary (3 sentences).
quests.teacherNote: Check irregular past forms (swam, ate, saw, flew) and sequencing words. Pairs can read their diary in nearby chat at the pond.

quests.title: Lost: One Magic Hat
quests.text: Write a "Lost!" poster for your magic hat. Say what it looks like, what it can do, and where you lost it. Useful phrases: "It is ... and ...", "It can ...", "I lost it near the ...". Post it in nearby chat and ask: "Did you see it?" Write your poster (3 sentences).
quests.teacherNote: Look for adjective order (a big purple hat) and "can" for abilities. Encourage classmates to reply with funny sightings ("I saw it at the cafe!").

quests.title: The Weekend Song
quests.text: Ask four classmates: "What are you going to do this weekend?" Real or silly answers are fine! Use them to write a song chorus. Useful phrases: "On Saturday, ... is going to ...", "We're going to have fun!" Post it in nearby chat. Write your chorus (3 lines).
quests.teacherNote: Check "is/are going to" + base verb. Give a bonus for rhymes (play/day, fun/sun).

quests.title: Soup Surprise
quests.text: Meet two classmates at the cafe and choose roles: customer, waiter and cook. Write a funny dialogue in nearby chat: something strange is in the soup! Useful phrases: "Excuse me, there's a ... in my soup!", "I'm so sorry!", "It's today's special!" Write your dialogue (at least 3 lines).
quests.teacherNote: Encourage silly objects (a tiny dinosaur, a sock) and polite phrases. Groups can perform their dialogue for the class at the cafe.

quests.title: Tongue Twister Trouble
quests.text: Choose a letter with a partner. Together, write a funny tongue twister where most words start with that letter, like "Six silly snakes sell socks." Whisper it to another classmate: "Can you type this fast?" Write your tongue twister and what happened.
quests.teacherNote: Check that the tongue twister is a real sentence (subject + verb + object). Later, ask volunteers to say theirs aloud in class for real pronunciation practice.

quests.title: Pixel Plaza Anthem
quests.text: Write a song for Pixel Plaza with two or three classmates. Each person chooses a favourite place in town and explains why in the chat. Turn the reasons into a 4-line chorus, then agree on the best order and a title. Useful phrases: "My favourite place is ... because ...", "What about putting ... first?", "I think this line sounds better because ..." Write your chorus with its title and one sentence explaining why you chose that order.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for reasons with "because" and polite agreeing and disagreeing while they order the lines. For a bonus, ask the group to make two lines rhyme.

quests.title: Mystery Box Story Chain
quests.text: Start a story in nearby chat at the cafe: "One morning, a mysterious box appeared on a table, and..." Ask at least four classmates to add one sentence each, and keep it going with follow-up questions like "What was inside?" or "What happened next?" Useful phrases: "Can you add the next part?", "I love your idea because..." Write the story in 4 sentences (shorten it if needed), then one more sentence: which idea did you like most, and why?
quests.teacherNote: Check past simple and linking words (then, suddenly, after that). If the cafe gets crowded, start a second chain at the hotel or the pond.

quests.title: Time Capsule Letter
quests.text: Write a letter with a partner for a time capsule that students will open in 2050. First, discuss: what is Pixel Plaza like today, and how will it be different? Compare your ideas. Useful phrases: "Today the cafe is ..., but in 2050 it will be ...", "I think the hotel will be bigger than ...", "Do you agree?" Write your letter in 4-5 sentences, starting "Dear students of 2050,".
quests.teacherNote: Look for "will" + comparatives (bigger, more modern, quieter). Pairs can whisper their letter to another pair and compare predictions.

quests.title: Haiku by the Bridge
quests.text: Go to the little bridge in the park and write a haiku about what you see: three lines of 5, 7 and 5 syllables, for example "Calm water below" (5). Use / between lines. Whisper it to two classmates and ask for their opinion, then improve one line. Useful phrases: "Which line do you like best, and why?", "Would you change anything?" Write your final haiku and two sentences about your classmates' feedback.
quests.teacherNote: Do not be strict about syllables; reward vivid words and clear feedback sentences ("She liked line 2 because..."). Show a model haiku first if the class has never seen one.

quests.title: Superhero of the Park
quests.text: Create a superhero who protects the park, together with two or three classmates. Each person suggests a name, a power and a funny weakness; then vote on the best ideas and give reasons. Useful phrases: "I prefer ... because ...", "Flying is cooler than ...", "Let's go with ..." Write a hero profile in 4-5 sentences: name, power, weakness, and how the hero saved the park last week.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for suggestions and reasons during the vote, and past simple in the rescue story. Groups can introduce their hero to the class at the fountain.

quests.title: Slogan Showdown
quests.text: Invent a new slogan for Pixel Plaza: the town council wants more visitors! Meet two or three classmates; each person proposes a slogan and persuades the others that theirs is the best. Then negotiate a final version that everyone accepts (combining ideas is allowed). Useful phrases: "The strongest thing about mine is...", "What if we kept your start and my ending?", "I see your point, but..." Write a short paragraph: your final slogan, the options you rejected, and why the group chose this one.
quests.teacherNote: Assess the persuasion and compromise language, not just the slogan itself. Finish with a quick class vote on all the final slogans.

quests.title: The Fussy Hotel Guest
quests.text: Write a comic dialogue with a partner at the hotel. One of you is an extremely fussy guest with a ridiculous complaint (the pond is too wet, the fountain is too loud); the other is a super-polite receptionist who must find a solution without ever saying no. Negotiate until you reach a deal. Useful phrases: "Would it help if we...?", "I'd only be happy if...", "How about... instead?" Act it out in whisper chat, then write a short paragraph summarising the complaint, the deal you reached and your funniest line.
quests.teacherNote: Look for hedged, polite offers ("Would it help if...") and conditions. Swap roles for a second round if there is time.

quests.title: If the Fountain Could Talk
quests.text: Give the fountain in the square a voice! Write a short monologue as the fountain: what it has seen, what it would do if it could move, and what it would ask the people walking past. Share it in nearby chat at the fountain and ask two classmates: "How would you react if the fountain really talked?" Useful phrases: "If I could ..., I would ...", "I've seen so many ...", "If it spoke to me, I'd ..." Write a short paragraph: your monologue plus a summary of your classmates' reactions.
quests.teacherNote: Check the second conditional (If I could..., I would...) and present perfect for experiences (I've seen...). Stronger students can add a reply from the pond or the bridge.

quests.title: Pixel Plaza: The Movie
quests.text: Write the trailer for a movie set in Pixel Plaza! First, mingle with at least four classmates and ask: What kind of film should it be (comedy, adventure, mystery...)? Who or what would the hero be? What would go wrong? Useful phrases: "Most people wanted..., although a few...", "If it were a comedy, the hero would..." Write a short paragraph summarising the different views, then your trailer voice-over, starting "In a town where..."
quests.teacherNote: Look for reporting language (most people, a few, while others) and a clear summary before the trailer. Volunteers can perform their trailer in nearby chat in the square.

quests.title: Shop of Impossible Things
quests.text: Open the Shop of Impossible Things with a partner: invent a product that cannot exist, like bottled sunshine or a jar of silence. Write a persuasive advert together, then persuade another classmate to try it; they should ask tough questions. Answer their doubts until they decide. Useful phrases: "Imagine never having to... again!", "If you tried it, you'd...", "I understand your concern, but..." Write a short paragraph: your advert, the customer's main doubt, and whether you convinced them.
quests.teacherNote: Look for persuasive structures and how students answer objections politely. Finish with a class vote for the most convincing impossible product.

quests.title: Meet Me There
quests.text: Pick a place, like the cafe. Whisper to a partner: "Meet me at the ...!" Walk there and say hello. Write: "I meet ... at the ... and we can see ..."
quests.teacherNote: Check the use of "at the" + place and simple greetings. For a quick extension, the partner chooses the next meeting place and they play again.

quests.title: Letter Jumble
quests.text: Put these letters in order to find a place in the Plaza: NUOTAFNI. Walk there and say in the nearby chat: "I am at the ...!" Then type the place.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: fountain (NUOTAFNI is FOUNTAIN with the letters mixed up). Fast finishers can mix up another place name, like PARK or HOTEL, and whisper it to a classmate to solve.

quests.title: Where Are You?
quests.text: Whisper "Where are you?" to four classmates. They answer: "I am at/near the ...". Write about two of them: "... is at the ... and ... is near the ..."
quests.teacherNote: Listen for "at the" vs "near the". Stronger students can try "between the ... and the ..." or "next to the ...".

quests.title: Look and Tell
quests.text: Go to the fountain or the pond. Look around: what colours and things do you see? Ask people nearby: "What can you see?" Write: "At the ..., I can see ... and ..."
quests.teacherNote: Answers depend on what each student really sees, so any honest description is correct. Encourage friendly replies in the chat like "I can see ... too!".

quests.title: My Top Spot
quests.text: Ask three classmates: "What is your favourite place in the Plaza?" Tell them your favourite too. Write: "My favourite place is the ... because it is ..." Add one sentence about a classmate.
quests.teacherNote: Encourage simple adjectives after "it is" (quiet, big, pretty, fun). A good classmate sentence is "... likes the ... because it is ...".

quests.title: Lost Tourist
quests.text: Meet a partner at the hotel. You are a lost tourist. Ask: "Excuse me, how do I get to the park?" Your partner gives directions and you follow them. Then swap roles. Useful phrases: go straight on, turn left/right, it's next to... Write 3 sentences: the directions you got and if they worked.
quests.teacherNote: Check that directions use imperatives and place phrases (next to, in front of, between). After the swap, the new tourist can ask for the cafe, the shop or the bridge.

quests.title: Plaza Hide and Seek
quests.text: Choose a secret place in the Plaza and go there. Whisper three clues to two or three classmates, but don't say the name! Useful phrases: "It's near the...", "You can ... there", "It has...". When they find you, say "Well done!" Write 3 sentences: your place, your clues and who found you.
quests.teacherNote: Good clues describe without naming the place (e.g. "You can drink hot chocolate there"). If seekers get stuck, the hider can give one extra clue with a direction.

quests.title: Next Stop Survey
quests.text: Ask four classmates: "Where are you going to go next?" and "What are you going to do there?" Tell them your plan too. Useful phrases: I'm going to walk to..., I'm going to meet... Write 3 sentences about their plans, like: "... is going to go to the ... to ..."
quests.teacherNote: Check "going to + verb" and "to + verb" for purpose (to buy a drink, to see the pond). As a follow-up, students can walk to a place a classmate mentioned and meet them there.

quests.title: Water Under My Feet
quests.text: Read this message from a friend: "I'm in the park. There is water under my feet, but I'm not wet!" Where is your friend? Check with a classmate: "Do you think it's the ...?" Walk there, then type the place.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: bridge (the little bridge in the park is the only place where you stand above water and stay dry). Fast finishers can write a similar message about another place and whisper it to a classmate.

quests.title: Tiny Tour Guide
quests.text: Be a tour guide! Take two or three classmates to three places in the Plaza. At each place, tell them one thing about it, like "This is the cafe. You can..." After the tour, write 3 sentences in the past simple: "First we went to... Then we... Finally..."
quests.teacherNote: Look for sequencing words (first, then, after that, finally) and past forms (went, saw, walked). To make it more interactive, the tourists ask the guide one question at each stop.

quests.title: Friday Meeting Spot
quests.text: Work with two or three classmates. Imagine you want to meet in the Plaza every Friday after school. Each person suggests a place and gives a reason. Compare the places and agree on one. Useful phrases: "I think the ... is better because...", "That's a good idea, but...", "What about the ...?" Then walk there together. Write 4 sentences: the places you compared, the place you chose and why.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for comparatives with reasons (quieter, closer, more fun) and polite disagreement. If the group cannot agree, they can vote and explain the result.

quests.title: Mystery Route
quests.text: Choose a secret destination, but don't tell your partner. Start together at the fountain. Whisper directions one step at a time; your partner follows them without knowing where they are going. Then swap. Useful phrases: "Walk past the...", "Keep going until you reach...", "It's on your left." Write 4 sentences: your directions, where your partner arrived, and which instruction was the most useful or the most confusing and why.
quests.teacherNote: Good directions use landmarks (past the cafe, until you reach the bridge) rather than only left/right, which depends on the way an avatar is facing. Ask pairs to share their most confusing instruction and improve it together.

quests.title: Live From the Plaza
quests.text: Be a TV reporter! Go to the square or the park and report what is happening right now. Describe what avatars are doing and wearing, and ask one person nearby: "What are you doing here today?" Useful phrases: "Right now, someone in a ... hat is...", "People are...", "It looks like..." Write a 4-sentence news report in the present continuous and add your opinion: is it a good place to be today, and why?
quests.teacherNote: Check present continuous forms (is walking, are chatting). Remind students to describe avatars kindly (hats, shirts, colours) and never comment on real people.

quests.title: Square vs Park
quests.text: Work with a partner. One of you goes to the square and the other goes to the park. Whisper to each other three things you can see. Then compare: which place is busier, quieter or more colourful? Ask a follow-up question, like "What is the best thing there?" Useful phrases: "The park is ...er than...", "Both places have...", "The square has..., but the park..." Write 4 sentences comparing the two places.
quests.teacherNote: Answers depend on what students see on the day, so any honest comparison is fine. Check comparative forms (busier, more colourful) and linkers like but, both and whereas.

quests.title: Plaza Find Someone Who
quests.text: Mingle and find a different classmate for each: someone who has walked over the bridge today, someone who prefers the cafe to the shop, someone who thinks the park is the best place, and someone who can explain the way from the hotel to the pond. Ask one follow-up question each time. Useful phrases: "Have you ... today?", "Do you prefer ... or ...?", "Can you tell me how to...?" Write 4 sentences about what you found out.
quests.teacherNote: Look for correct question forms (Have you walked...? Do you prefer...?) and genuine follow-up questions. In a small class or at the start of a session, let students use the same classmate twice or write "Nobody has... yet".

quests.title: Mayor for a Day
quests.text: Imagine the mayor of Pixel Plaza can add only one new thing: maybe a cinema, a skate park, an ice-cream stand, or your own idea. In a group of three or four, each person picks a different idea and tries to persuade the others. Explain where in the Plaza it would go and who it would help. Then negotiate one final choice. Useful phrases: "If we built..., people could...", "I see your point, but...", "What if we compromised and...?" Write a short paragraph summarising each person's proposal, the main arguments, and how your group reached its decision.
quests.teacherNote: Look for second conditionals (If we built..., it would...) and polite negotiation language. Groups can walk to the spot where they would put their idea while arguing, which makes their reasons more concrete.

quests.title: Festival Planners
quests.text: Plan a festival in Pixel Plaza: a chestnut festival (Castanyada), a friendly Halloween party, Saint George's Day, or another celebration you like. Mingle and ask at least four classmates for one activity idea each and where it should happen (the square, the cafe, the park...). Discuss the ideas and persuade people to support your favourites. Useful phrases: "The square would be perfect for... because...", "That might be too..., so how about...?" Write a short paragraph presenting your festival plan: the best ideas, where they go, where people disagreed, and why you chose them.
quests.teacherNote: The chat only accepts English, so students should type "chestnut festival" or "Saint George's Day" rather than Catalan names. Look for suggestions backed by reasons and a summary that includes at least one different opinion.

quests.title: Suitcase Trouble
quests.text: Imagine a tourist with a huge, heavy suitcase arrives at the hotel and wants to sit by the pond in the park. With a partner, each of you walks a different route and checks it: Is it short? Is it easy? Is anything in the way? Then compare your routes and agree on the best one. Useful phrases: "My route is longer, but it's much easier because...", "If the tourist went that way, they'd have to...", "On balance, I'd recommend..." Write a short paragraph giving clear directions for the best route and explaining why it is better than the other one.
quests.teacherNote: If there is only one obvious path, one partner can take a detour (for example past the cafe or across the square) so there is something to compare. Look for clear sequenced directions plus a balanced justification (longer but easier, shorter but busier).

quests.title: The Great Cake Mystery
quests.text: Solve a mystery: the cafe's prize-winning cake has disappeared! The suspects are a hungry seagull, a sleepy giant and a cake-loving robot. Mingle and interview at least four classmates as witnesses: "Where were you at the time, and what were you doing?" "What did you notice?" Witnesses can invent their stories, but they must stay consistent. Useful phrases: "It can't have been the... because...", "The ... must have...", "One witness claimed that..., whereas..." Write a short paragraph summarising the statements and explaining who you think took the cake.
quests.teacherNote: The suspects are fictional, so no classmate is ever accused; classmates are only witnesses. Look for must have / can't have / might have and past continuous in the witness answers, and reward students who spot contradictions between statements.

quests.title: Plaza Time Machine
quests.text: Imagine Pixel Plaza 100 years in the past or 100 years in the future. Walk with a partner to three places and discuss how each one might have looked then, or might look in the future. Would the cafe still exist? What would replace the shop? Challenge each other's ideas with follow-up questions. Useful phrases: "A hundred years ago, there would probably have been...", "In the future, this might become...", "I doubt it, because..." Write a short paragraph comparing your ideas and your partner's, and say which version of the Plaza you would rather visit and why.
quests.teacherNote: Look for speculative language (might have been, would probably, could become) and a genuine comparison of two viewpoints. Weaker pairs can choose only the future, which needs simpler forms (will, might).

quests.title: Hat Hunt
quests.text: Walk around and find 3 avatars with a hat. Ask them: "Do you like your hat?" Write 2 sentences like this: "... has a ... hat. ... likes it."
quests.teacherNote: Check that students use 'has' for the third person and put the colour before the noun ('a green hat'). If only a few avatars wear hats, let students ask about glasses instead.

quests.title: My Look, Your Look
quests.text: Tell a classmate about your avatar in nearby chat: "I have ... hair and a ... shirt." Ask: "And you?" Write 2 sentences: "I have ..." and "My classmate has ..."
quests.teacherNote: Look for the change from 'I have' to 'my classmate has' and for the right word order ('a red shirt', not 'a shirt red'). Stronger students can add glasses or a hat.

quests.title: Colour Twins
quests.text: Walk around and find a classmate with the same shirt colour or hair colour as you. Ask: "Is your shirt/hair ...?" Write: "My colour twin is ... . We both have ... ."
quests.teacherNote: This practises 'both' and colour words. If a student can't find an exact match, let them choose the closest colour ('We both have dark hair').

quests.title: Secret Avatar
quests.text: Stand with a classmate. Pick a secret avatar you can both see. Whisper: "This avatar has ... hair and a ... shirt." Your classmate guesses. Write: "The secret avatar is ... . The guess is right/wrong."
quests.teacherNote: Pairs need to stand close together so they both see the same avatars. Stronger students can add a third clue about glasses or a hat.

quests.title: Dream Hat
quests.text: Imagine a new hat for your avatar. Tell a classmate in nearby chat: "My dream hat is ... because ..." Then ask: "And you?" Write 1-2 sentences about your dream hat.
quests.teacherNote: Encourage two adjectives in the right order ('a big purple hat') and a simple reason with 'because'. Fast finishers can imagine their dream glasses too.

quests.title: Fountain Prize Puzzle
quests.text: Solve the puzzle. Nora wears a red hat and no glasses. Pablo wears glasses and no hat. Kim has no hat and no glasses. Zoe wears a hat and glasses. The prize goes to the avatar with glasses but no hat. Who wins? Whisper to a classmate: "It's ... because ..." Then type the name.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: Pablo. He is the only avatar with glasses and no hat (Zoe has both, Nora has only a hat, Kim has neither). Students whisper their reason so they don't spoil the answer for others in nearby chat.

quests.title: Fashion Reporter
quests.text: Be a fashion reporter in the square. Ask 4 classmates about their avatars: "Why did you choose your hair colour?" and "What do you like best about your avatar?" Useful phrases: "I chose it because ...", "I like my ... best." Write 3 sentences: who you asked and what they said.
quests.teacherNote: Look for correct past simple questions ('Why did you choose...?') and the third person in the report ('Marc chose blue because...'). Remind reporters that every answer is a good answer.

quests.title: Spot the Difference
quests.text: Stand next to a classmate and compare your avatars. Find 3 differences and tell your classmate. Useful phrases: "My shirt is ..., but your shirt is ...", "You have glasses, but I don't." Then find one thing you both have. Write 3 sentences: 2 differences and 1 thing that is the same.
quests.teacherNote: Check that students use 'but' for contrast and short negatives ('I don't', 'mine isn't'). Stronger pairs can add 'both' and 'neither'.

quests.title: Party Look Planners
quests.text: Choose a celebration with 2 classmates: Halloween, the chestnut festival (Castanyada), Saint George's Day or another one you like. Plan your avatars' looks for it: hats, glasses, hair and shirt colours. Useful phrases: "I'm going to wear ...", "What are you going to wear?" Write 3 sentences: one about each person's look.
quests.teacherNote: Look for 'going to' and clothes and colour words. Festival names in answers should be in English (chestnut festival, Saint George's Day), and Halloween looks should stay fun, not scary.

quests.title: The Pixel Boutique
quests.text: Meet a classmate at the shop. One of you is the shop assistant; the other is a customer who wants a new hat or glasses. Useful phrases: "Can I help you?", "Have you got it in blue?", "It looks great!" Then swap roles. Write 3 sentences: what you wanted and what you chose.
quests.teacherNote: The shopping is pretend, so no game money or items are needed. Look for polite requests and past simple in the journal ('I wanted a red hat, but I chose a blue one').

quests.title: Cafe Colour Mystery
quests.text: Solve the puzzle. In the cafe, Ava, Ben, Cleo and Dan each wear a different shirt colour: red, blue, green or yellow. Dan's shirt is the same colour as a banana. Ava's shirt is neither red nor blue. Ben's shirt is neither red nor green. What colour is Cleo's shirt? Whisper your reasoning to a classmate. Useful phrases: "It can't be ... because ...", "So ... must be ..." Then type the colour.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: red. Dan is yellow (banana), so Ava must be green and Ben must be blue, which leaves red for Cleo. Ask students to explain it using 'must' and 'can't'.

quests.title: Plaza Fashion Awards
quests.text: Organise the Plaza Fashion Awards. Invent 2 positive categories, for example "Coolest Glasses" or "Most Colourful Avatar". Ask at least 4 classmates to vote in each category, then ask a follow-up question: "Why that one?" Useful phrases: "I'd vote for ... because ...", "For me, ... has the coolest ... because ..." Write 3-5 sentences: the winners and the best reasons people gave.
quests.teacherNote: Check superlatives (coolest, most colourful) and reasons that go beyond 'because it's nice'. If several students do this quest, encourage lots of different categories so that many avatars win something.

quests.title: Yes-No Detectives
quests.text: Play "Who Am I?" with 2 or 3 classmates. One player secretly chooses an avatar everyone can see in the square. The others ask only yes/no questions, for example "Is this avatar wearing glasses?" or "Is the shirt darker than mine?" Count the questions and take turns. Useful phrases: "Does it have ...?", "Is it the one near the fountain?" Write 3-5 sentences: who guessed fastest, how many questions you needed, and the most useful question.
quests.teacherNote: Listen for 'Is ... wearing...?' and 'Does ... have...?' questions and comparatives. To make it harder, ban colour words for the first three questions.

quests.title: Right Look, Right Place
quests.text: Compare your avatar with a classmate's avatar. Decide together whose avatar is better dressed for three situations: a picnic by the pond, a fancy party at the hotel and a rainy morning at the cafe. Give reasons and ask follow-up questions like "Why do you think so?" Useful phrases: "Your avatar is better dressed for ... because ...", "Mine is more ... than yours", "I see your point, but ..." Write 3-5 sentences comparing the two avatars.
quests.teacherNote: Look for comparatives (brighter, more formal, better) and reasons linked to each situation. Keep it light: ideally each avatar wins at least one situation.

quests.title: Future Fashion 2100
quests.text: Imagine Pixel Plaza in the year 2100. What will avatars wear? Ask 2 or 3 classmates for their predictions about hats, glasses, hair and shirts, and ask a follow-up question about each idea. Useful phrases: "I think avatars will wear ...", "Maybe they won't need ... because ...", "Cool idea! Why ...?" Write 3-5 sentences: the best predictions and which idea you liked most, with a reason.
quests.teacherNote: Look for 'will/won't' for predictions and genuine follow-up questions. Groups that finish early can design one complete 2100 look together and post it in nearby chat.

quests.title: Team Parade Look
quests.text: Imagine your group of 3-4 is entering the Pixel Plaza Team Parade and needs one team look. Each person proposes a look (hair colour, hat, glasses, shirt colour) and tries to persuade the others. Then negotiate: you can combine ideas, but everyone must accept the final look. Useful phrases: "What if we ...?", "I could live with ... as long as ...", "Would you agree to ... if we ...?" Write a short paragraph: the proposals, the arguments that changed people's minds, and the final team look and team name.
quests.teacherNote: Look for negotiation language (conditionals, 'as long as', compromise) and a paragraph that reports different views, not just the final result. Make sure every member's proposal is heard.

quests.title: One Colour for All
quests.text: Debate an imaginary new law: "From next week, every avatar in Pixel Plaza must wear the same shirt colour." Is it fair, fun or a terrible idea? Ask at least 4 classmates what they think and why, and politely challenge each one with a "What if ...?" question. Useful phrases: "If this law existed, ...", "On the one hand ..., on the other hand ...", "Some people argued that ..., while others felt ..." Write a short paragraph summarising the different views and giving your own balanced opinion.
quests.teacherNote: Look for second conditionals ('If everyone wore red, ...') and a paragraph that reports several views fairly before giving an opinion. You can swap in another silly law, e.g. 'Glasses are banned at the pond'.

quests.title: Avatar Makeover Show
quests.text: Run a TV-style makeover show with a classmate. The host interviews the guest about their avatar: what they love about its look and what they would change if they could. Then the host suggests one makeover idea and tries to persuade the guest, who can accept, refuse or negotiate. Keep it kind. Swap roles. Useful phrases: "If you swapped your ... for ..., you'd ...", "Have you ever considered ...?", "I'm not sure that would suit my avatar because ..." Write a short paragraph: both makeover ideas, the arguments used, and whether each guest said yes.
quests.teacherNote: Look for tactful persuasion and conditionals ('If you swapped..., you'd...'). Remind hosts that the guest always decides, so a polite 'no thanks' is a good ending too.

quests.title: Riddle of the Square
quests.text: Write a riddle about one avatar you can see in the square (not your own) using creative clues instead of plain colour words, for example: "This avatar's hat is the colour of a ripe tomato, and its glasses would suit a famous detective." Whisper it to at least 4 classmates, one by one, and see who can guess the name. Keep every clue kind. Write a short paragraph: your riddle, how many classmates guessed it, which clue helped most, and what you would change if you did it again.
