quests.teacherNote: Reward imaginative comparisons ('as bright as a traffic light', 'the colour of a ripe tomato') over plain colour words. Check that clues describe only the avatar's clothes and colours and are always kind.

quests.title: Launch Your Brand
quests.text: Invent a fashion brand for avatars, sold at the Pixel Plaza shop. Decide its name, a slogan and one signature item (a hat, glasses or a shirt), and think about who would wear it and where. Post your slogan in nearby chat and ask 2 classmates: "Would you buy this? What would make it better?" Useful phrases: "Imagine walking into the cafe wearing ...", "It's perfect for anyone who ...", "Unlike other brands, ours ..." Write a short paragraph pitching your brand and summarising the feedback you got.
quests.teacherNote: Look for persuasive techniques (addressing the reader directly, 'Imagine...', contrast with 'unlike') and a fair summary of the feedback, including criticism. Brand names should be invented, not real ones.

quests.title: The Thumb Riddle
quests.text: Solve this riddle: "I have a thumb and four fingers, but I am not a hand. You wear me in winter. What am I?" Type: "It is a ..." Then tell a classmate the riddle.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: glove (it has a thumb and four fingers but is not a hand). Extend by asking students to name more winter clothes, e.g. scarf, hat, coat.

quests.title: Head, Foot and Legs
quests.text: Find a partner. Read this riddle together: "I have a head, a foot and four legs, but I am not an animal. You sleep on me." Ask: "Is it a ...?" Type the answer.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: bed (a bed has a head, a foot and four legs). Point out the double meanings: the head and foot of a bed, the legs of a bed or table.

quests.title: Face and Hands
quests.text: Meet two or three classmates. Share this riddle: "I have a face and two hands, but no arms and no legs." Everyone writes: "I think it is a ..." Agree and type the answer.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: clock (watch is also accepted): it has a face and two hands. A good moment to review body words that also describe objects.

quests.title: Keys but No Doors
quests.text: Solve the riddle: "I have keys, but I open no doors. You play music on me." Then ask four classmates: "What am I?" Type the answer: "It is a ..."
quests.teacherNote: Answer: piano (keyboard, organ and accordion are also accepted, as they also have keys). Ask fast finishers to name other instruments in English.

quests.title: The Third Child
quests.text: Ask a classmate this riddle: "Tom's mum has three children. One is April. One is May. What is the name of the third child?" Read it slowly! Type: "The third child is ..."
quests.teacherNote: Answer: Tom. Many people say June because of April and May, but the answer is in the first word. Use it to revise the months and the possessive 's.

quests.title: Tea Time Puzzle
quests.text: Go to the cafe with a partner. Solve this riddle together: "What starts with T, ends with T and is full of T?" Hint: you can find it in the cafe. Useful phrases: "Maybe it's a ...", "No, because ...", "You're right!" Type the answer.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: teapot. It starts and ends with the letter T and is full of tea, which sounds like 'T'. Extension: pairs invent their own 'starts with... ends with...' riddle.

quests.title: Odd or Even?
quests.text: Solve this number riddle: "I am an odd number. Take away one letter from my name and I become even." Hint: spell the odd numbers in English: one, three, five... Then whisper the riddle to a classmate. Can they solve it? Type: "The number is ..."
quests.teacherNote: Answer: seven (7): take away the S and 'seven' becomes 'even'. Check that students know 'odd' (1, 3, 5...) and 'even' (2, 4, 6...) before they start.

quests.title: Walk in the Park
quests.text: Go to the park with two or three classmates. Walk over the little bridge together. Then solve this riddle: "The more you take, the more you leave behind. What are they?" Hint: you took some on the bridge. Useful phrases: "I think they are ...", "Good idea!", "I don't agree." Type the answer.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: footsteps (steps and footprints are also accepted): the more steps you take, the more you leave behind you. Listen for agreeing and disagreeing phrases in the group chat.

quests.title: The Calendar Trap
quests.text: Ask four classmates this riddle: "Some months have 30 days and some have 31. How many months have 28 days?" Count how many classmates say "one". Then think again carefully! Useful phrases: "What's your answer?", "Are you sure?" Type: "... months have 28 days."
quests.teacherNote: Answer: all twelve months have at least 28 days; 'one' (February) is the trap. Follow up by asking how many classmates fell into the trap, e.g. 'Three people said one.'

quests.title: The Strange Room
quests.text: Solve this riddle: "I am a room, but I have no doors, no windows and no walls. Some people love me on pizza. What am I?" Then ask a classmate if they agree. Useful phrase: "I think it's a ... because ..." Type the answer.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: mushroom (the word ends in 'room', but it has no doors, windows or walls). Extension: ask students to find other words with a smaller word hidden inside, e.g. pancake, butterfly.

quests.title: Minute and Moment
quests.text: Solve this classic riddle: "What comes once in a minute, twice in a moment, but never in a thousand years?" Hint: don't think about time, think about spelling. When you know the answer, test it on a classmate in nearby chat and give hints if they get stuck. Useful phrases: "Have you noticed that ...?", "Look at the letters in ..." Type your answer as a full sentence: "It is the letter ..."
quests.teacherNote: Answer: the letter M (one M in 'minute', two in 'moment', none in 'a thousand years'). Students must type 'the letter M' because a single letter cannot be checked safely, so a bare 'M' is not accepted.

quests.title: The Whisper Riddle
quests.text: Whisper this riddle to a partner: "If you have me, you want to share me. If you share me, you don't have me anymore. What am I?" Discuss your ideas and give reasons. Which answer fits better, yours or your partner's? Useful phrases: "It can't be ... because ...", "I think it's ... because ...", "That makes sense!" Type the answer you agree on.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: a secret (once you share it, it is not a secret any more). If someone suggests 'a surprise', discuss why 'secret' fits better, and remind students not to share any real secrets.

quests.title: The Shrinking Word
quests.text: Solve this riddle: "Which five-letter English word becomes shorter when you add two letters to it?" Hint: think about what the longer word means. Then ask at least four classmates for their answers in nearby chat. Who found the trick first, and whose explanation is the clearest? Useful phrases: "What did you get?", "Your answer is cleverer than mine because ..." Type: "The word is ..."
quests.teacherNote: Answer: short (add -er and you get 'shorter'). Use it as a way into comparatives: ask students for other adjectives that take -er.

quests.title: Arriving on Friday
quests.text: Meet two or three classmates at the fountain. Discuss this riddle: "A cowboy rode into Pixel Plaza on Friday. He stayed at the hotel for three nights, and then he left on Friday. How is that possible?" Share ideas and ask follow-up questions. Useful phrases: "What if ...?", "Why do you think so?", "That can't be right because ..." Type one short sentence that explains the trick.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: Friday is the name of the cowboy's horse, so he rode in on Friday and rode out on Friday. Any short sentence containing 'horse' is accepted; if groups get stuck, hint that 'on Friday' can have two meanings.

quests.title: Riddle Maker
quests.text: Write a "What am I?" riddle about something in Pixel Plaza, for example in the cafe, hotel, shop or park. Give three clues, from difficult to easy. Whisper it to a partner one clue at a time. After how many clues did they guess? Then swap roles. Useful phrases: "Here's my first clue: ...", "Do you want another clue?", "You got it!" Write 3-5 sentences: your riddle, your partner's guesses and the answer.
quests.teacherNote: Look for clear describing language (I am made of..., You use me to..., You can find me in...) and clues that really go from difficult to easy. Fast pairs can try a second riddle with only two clues.

quests.title: The Lobby Clock
quests.text: Solve this logic riddle, then challenge a classmate: "The old clock in the hotel lobby rings six times at six o'clock, with equal gaps between the rings. From the first ring to the last takes exactly five seconds. How long does it take from the first ring to the last at twelve o'clock?" Careful: the obvious answer is wrong. If a classmate disagrees with you, try to persuade them with a clear explanation. Useful phrases: "If six rings take ..., then ...", "The key point is that ..." Type the number of seconds.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: 11 seconds. Six rings have five gaps (one second each); twelve rings have eleven gaps, so the answer is 11, not the 'obvious' 10.

quests.title: Fox, Chicken and Corn
quests.text: Meet a partner on the little bridge in the park and solve this classic puzzle: "A farmer must take a fox, a chicken and a bag of corn across a river. Her boat can carry her and only one of them. If she leaves the fox and the chicken alone, the fox eats the chicken. If she leaves the chicken and the corn alone, the chicken eats the corn." Plan the trips together and test each idea. Useful phrases: "What if she took ... first?", "That wouldn't work because ...", "So the next step is ..." Then answer: in the shortest plan, which of the three things crosses the river three times (each way counts)?
quests.teacherNote: Answer: the chicken. Shortest plan: take the chicken over, go back, take the fox (or the corn) over, bring the chicken back, take the corn (or the fox) over, go back, take the chicken over again, so the chicken crosses three times and the others once; listen for 'If she took..., the ... would...'.

quests.title: Bankrupt at the Hotel
quests.text: Meet two or three classmates in the hotel and solve this lateral-thinking riddle: "A man pushes his car to a hotel. As soon as he arrives, he tells the owner that he is bankrupt (he has no money left). Why?" Hint: nobody is really sad, and the car is tiny. Take turns suggesting explanations and testing them. Before you decide, one person summarises the group's ideas. Useful phrases: "What if he were ...?", "That doesn't explain why ...", "So far, we think ..." Type one short sentence that explains what is really happening.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: he is playing Monopoly: his token is the little car, he lands on a street with a hotel and cannot pay the rent. Answers naming Monopoly or 'a board game' are accepted.

quests.title: Triple Double Trouble
quests.text: Work with at least four classmates in nearby chat to crack this word puzzle: "Which English word has three double letters in a row, like the made-up word aabbcc?" Hint: it is a job. This person keeps the money records of a business, such as a hotel. Everyone suggests words with double letters (coffee? balloon? committee?) and explains why each one does or doesn't work. Before you type, summarise which ideas you ruled out and why. Useful phrases: "That's close, but ...", "Let's rule out ...", "So far, we've found ..." Type the word.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: bookkeeper (oo-kk-ee); 'bookkeeping' also works. 'Coffee' (only two pairs in a row) and 'committee' (three pairs, but not in a row) are good near misses to discuss.

quests.title: Riddle Champion
quests.text: Write your own original riddle about something everyone in class knows (not a person), such as an object, an animal or a place in Pixel Plaza. Try it on at least four classmates in nearby chat, and give one extra clue only if they ask for it. Notice who solved it, how quickly, and which clue helped most. Then improve your riddle so it is fair but still tricky. Useful phrases: "Would it help if I told you ...?", "Most people thought ..., but ..." Write a short paragraph: your final riddle, how your classmates reacted, and what you changed and why.
quests.teacherNote: Good answers summarise several classmates' reactions and explain the changes, e.g. removing a clue that made it too easy. You could collect the best riddles for a class riddle competition.

quests.title: Secret Place Scramble
quests.text: Unscramble the letters N-T-A-I-N-F-O-U to find a place in Pixel Plaza. Walk there and write in nearby chat: "I am at the ...!" Then type the place in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: fountain (in the square). Check the nearby chat to see who reached it; to reuse the quest, scramble another place, e.g. B-I-D-E-G-R (bridge).

quests.title: Cafe Odd One Out
quests.text: Find the odd one out: milk, juice, bread, water, tea. Ask two classmates in nearby chat: "Which word is different?" Say: "I think it is ..." Type the odd word in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: bread, because it is food and the others are drinks. Fast finishers can add a reason with "because" in the chat.

quests.title: Opposite Animal Code
quests.text: Find the opposites of up, young and bad. Their first letters, in order, spell an animal. Ask a classmate: "What is the opposite of ...?" Type the animal in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: down, old, good, so the animal is DOG. Remind students to type the animal, not the three opposites (those alone are marked wrong).

quests.title: The Magic Word
quests.text: Find one word that goes after foot, basket and snow to make three new words. Write in nearby chat: "My words are ..." Type the magic word in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: ball (football, basketball, snowball); the three compound words are also accepted. Fast finishers can find more ball words, such as handball or volleyball, and share them in nearby chat.

quests.title: Class Fruit Salad
quests.text: Ask four classmates: "Can you name a fruit?" Every fruit must be different! Then write 1-2 sentences in your journal: "My class fruit salad has ..., ... and ..."
quests.teacherNote: Check the spelling of the fruit names and that each one is different. Reuse the quest by changing the category to vegetables, animals or clothes.

quests.title: Hungry Word Chain
quests.text: Play a food word chain with two or three classmates in nearby chat. The next food must start with the last letter of the food before (apple, egg, grapes...). No repeats! Useful phrases: "Your turn!", "Is that a food?" Write 2-3 sentences: how many words your chain had and which word was the best.
quests.teacherNote: Read the nearby chat to check spelling and that each word follows the last-letter rule. For a harder version, ban plurals or change the topic to animals or countries.

quests.title: Word Glue
quests.text: With a classmate, find one word that goes before bow, coat and drop to make three new words. Useful phrases: "What about ...?", "I don't think so.", "Yes, that works!" Then make a puzzle like this one for your partner. Type the secret word in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: rain (rainbow, raincoat, raindrop); the full compound words are also accepted. A good partner puzzle has only one answer, e.g. sun (sunglasses, sunflower, sunshine).

quests.title: The Odd Verb Out
quests.text: Look at these past simple verbs: went, saw, played, ate, took. One is different. Which one? Clue: think about how we make the past. Then post the puzzle in nearby chat and see if a classmate can solve it. Useful phrase: "Can you find the odd one?" Type the odd verb in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: played, the only regular (-ed) verb; went, saw, ate and took are irregular. Fast finishers can write the opposite puzzle: one irregular verb among regular ones.

quests.title: Hidden Animal Hunt
quests.text: One animal is hiding in all these words: VA _ _ _ ION, EDU _ _ _ ION, LO _ _ _ ION. Find it! Then ask four classmates in nearby chat: "Which animal is hiding in vacation, education and location?" Who answers first? Type the animal in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: cat (vacation, education, location). Ask early finishers for more words with cat inside, such as catch, category or caterpillar.

quests.title: Ship to Stop
quests.text: Change one letter at a time to go from SHIP to STOP: SHIP, ?, STOP. The middle word is a place in Pixel Plaza. Then write your own ladder (like HOT, ?, CAT) and whisper it to a classmate. Useful phrases: "Change one letter.", "Is that a word?" Type the middle word in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: SHOP (SHIP, SHOP, STOP); the other route, STIP, is not a word, so the answer is unique. Check that students' own ladders change only one letter at each step.

quests.title: Prefix Detective
quests.text: Make the opposite of each adjective by adding a prefix: happy, kind, polite, friendly, fair. One word needs a different prefix from the others. Which one? Compare your answer with a classmate and explain your reasons. Useful phrases: "I think the odd one is ... because ...", "Do you agree?", "What about ...?" Type the odd adjective in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: polite, because its opposite is impolite while the others take un- (unhappy, unkind, unfriendly, unfair); impolite is also accepted. Extend with dis- and il- words such as dishonest and illegal.

quests.title: Listen Carefully
quests.text: Rearrange all the letters of LISTEN to make a new word that means "with no sound at all". Then go to the place in Pixel Plaza you think is the most peaceful and tell classmates nearby why. Useful phrases: "It's quieter than ...", "I prefer it because ..." Type the new word in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: SILENT (the same six letters as LISTEN; silence is not accepted because it is not an anagram). Listen for comparatives in the chat; extra anagram pairs for fast finishers: EARTH/HEART, NIGHT/THING.

quests.title: The Wettest Riddle
quests.text: Solve this riddle: "What gets wetter and wetter the more it dries?" (Clue: you can find one in every hotel bathroom.) Before you type, ask at least four classmates in nearby chat for their guesses and ask follow-up questions to check their ideas. Useful phrases: "What's your guess?", "Why do you think that?", "That's clever, but ..." Type the answer in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: a towel (it dries you, so it gets wet). Only towel is accepted, so if students argue for a sponge, praise the reasoning and discuss why towel fits better.

quests.title: Sweet Idiom Puzzle
quests.text: Find the one food word that completes all three expressions: "a piece of ___" (very easy), "the icing on the ___" (the best extra thing) and "you can't have your ___ and eat it" (you can't have everything you want). Work with a classmate, then discuss which expression is the most useful and why. Useful phrases: "I'd use this one when ...", "I prefer ... because ..." Type the food word in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: cake (a piece of cake, the icing on the cake, you can't have your cake and eat it). Listen for the idioms used in real examples, and follow up with other food idioms such as "spill the beans".

quests.title: Mystery Word
quests.text: Play "Mystery Word" with two or three classmates. One player secretly chooses an object you can find in Pixel Plaza, like something in the cafe or the park. The others ask yes/no questions in nearby chat to guess it, with a maximum of 15 questions. Take turns. Useful phrases: "Is it bigger than ...?", "Can you eat it?", "Is it used for ...?" Write 3-5 sentences: which words you guessed, how many questions it took, and which question was the most helpful.
quests.teacherNote: Look for correctly formed yes/no questions and comparatives in the chat. Make it harder with a 10-question limit or a ban on colour questions.

quests.title: The Shrinking Word
quests.text: Solve this riddle with two or three classmates: "Which five-letter word becomes shorter when you add two letters to it?" Each person suggests an answer in nearby chat and tries to persuade the others it is right. If you disagree, explain your reasoning and listen to the other arguments before you decide together. Think about the meaning of the riddle, not only the spelling. Useful phrases: "I'm convinced it's ... because ...", "That's a fair point, but ...", "What if the answer is ...?" Type your group's answer, the five-letter word, in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: SHORT, because short + er = shorter. Listen for persuasion and polite disagreement; groups that finish early can invent a similar riddle for another group.

quests.title: One Small Word
quests.text: Find the one small word that completes all three sentences: "We've run ___ of milk, so I'll buy some at the shop." "Can you help me work ___ the answer to this puzzle?" "I was shocked when I found ___ the truth." Whisper a classmate to compare answers. Then each of you writes one more sentence with a phrasal verb using the same word; decide together which sentence sounds more natural and why. Useful phrases: "I'd say it's ... because ...", "Wouldn't ... sound more natural?" Type the missing word in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: out (run out of, work out, find out); "on" fits the second sentence but not the first, which makes a good discussion point. Check the extra sentences for natural phrasal verbs such as sort out, go out or check out.

quests.title: Three Meanings, One Word
quests.text: Find one English word with all three of these meanings: a season of the year; a place where water comes up naturally out of the ground; and a metal coil that jumps back when you press it. When you have it, invent a similar three-meaning clue for another word with several meanings (for example "light", "match" or "bat") and post it in nearby chat. If a classmate guesses it, ask them which meaning they found easiest and why. Useful phrases: "Here's a tricky one for you...", "Which meaning gave it away?" Type the word with three meanings in your journal.
quests.teacherNote: Solution: spring (the season, a water spring, a metal spring). Check that the clues students post have only one answer; good models are match (a game, a fire stick, to go well together) and light (not heavy, not dark, a lamp).

quests.title: Desert Island Dictionary
quests.text: Imagine your group is on a desert island and can only keep five English words; every other word disappears forever. With two or three classmates, negotiate in nearby chat which five words to keep. Each person proposes two words and tries to persuade the others, then you must agree on a final list. Useful phrases: "If we lost ..., we couldn't ...", "I see your point, but ...", "Shall we compromise on ...?" Write a short paragraph: your final five words, the best argument you heard, and one word you were sad to lose and why.
quests.teacherNote: Look for second conditional sentences, persuasion and compromise in the chat. Adapt it by limiting the list to verbs or adjectives, or by changing the number of words.

quests.title: New Words for Pixel Plaza
quests.text: Invent a new compound word for something in Pixel Plaza that has no name yet, for example "lift-wait" (the feeling of waiting ages for the hotel lift) or "fountain-walker" (someone who walks round the fountain all day). Write it with a hyphen. Explain your word to at least four classmates in nearby chat, listen to theirs and vote for the best one. Useful phrases: "It would be perfect for ...", "Mine is catchier because ...", "Yours is clever, but ..." Write a short paragraph: your word and its meaning, the best word you heard, and why it got your vote.
quests.teacherNote: Check that invented words are kind and not aimed at real classmates. If the chat filter blocks a new word, students can type the two parts separately (lift wait).

quests.title: Guess My Costume
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Think of a carnival costume. Don't tell! Your partner asks questions like "Are you a pirate?" Answer "Yes, I am" or "No, I'm not." Then swap. Write: "My partner is a ..."
quests.teacherNote: Listen for "Are you a ...?" and the short answers. If a pair gets stuck, allow category hints like "It's an animal."

quests.title: Ice Cream Survey
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Ask four classmates: "What ice cream do you like in summer?" Answer the question too. Is chocolate the winner? Write: "... classmates like ... and my favourite is ..."
quests.teacherNote: Expect flavours like chocolate, vanilla, strawberry and lemon. Teach "flavour" if needed, and check "like" after plural subjects ("Two classmates like...").

quests.title: Spring Word Chain
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Meet two or three classmates in the park. Take turns in the chat: say one spring word, like "flower" or "rain". No repeats! Can you get ten? Then write: "Our spring words are ..."
quests.teacherNote: Expect words like sun, flowers, birds, rain, trees and butterflies. For a harder round, allow only adjectives, or only words that start with one letter.

quests.title: Pack for Camp
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Imagine you go to summer camp. Ask a classmate: "What is in your bag?" Answer too. Pack one funny thing! Write: "My partner's bag has a ..., a ... and a ..."
quests.teacherNote: Help with camp words (torch or flashlight, sleeping bag, tent, toothbrush, sun cream) and enjoy the funny items. Check "has" in the sentence they write.

quests.title: Fire and Wings Riddle
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Read the riddle: "I am big and green. I have wings and I breathe fire. Saint George fights me. What am I?" Ask a classmate to guess too. Type: "You are a ..."
quests.teacherNote: Answer: dragon. It is the creature in the Saint George's Day (Sant Jordi) legend, so this is a quick way into the story.

quests.title: Easter Break Plans
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Ask three classmates: "What are you going to do in the Easter break?" Then ask one more question, like "Where?" or "Why?" Plans at home are great too! Useful phrases: "I'm going to ...", "That sounds fun!" Write 3 sentences: who you asked and their plans.
quests.teacherNote: Check "going to + verb" in the reports (e.g. "Pau is going to visit his cousins"). Students with no plans can describe a relaxing week at home or make up a dream plan.

quests.title: The Costume Shop
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Go to the shop with a partner. One of you is the shop assistant; the other wants a carnival costume. Ask about colour and size. Then swap. Useful phrases: "Can I help you?", "I'm looking for ...", "Can I try it on?" Write 3 sentences: what costume you chose and why.
quests.teacherNote: Look for polite shop phrases and clothes and colour words. No prices are needed. Fast pairs can add a problem to solve, like the wrong size or no more pirate hats.

quests.title: Midsummer Beach Party
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Plan a Midsummer (Sant Joan) beach party, or another summer party you like, with two or three classmates. Agree on food, music and one fun activity. Useful phrases: "Let's ...", "What about ...?", "Good idea!" Write 3 sentences with "We are going to ..."
quests.teacherNote: Typical Sant Joan ideas in English are a bonfire, fireworks, sweet bread (coca) and music on the beach. Check that every member of the group suggests at least one idea.

quests.title: Hidden Holiday Word
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Find the hidden word! Take the first letter of each answer: a Saint George's Day present with pages; the opposite of "start" (3 letters); the month of Saint George's Day; you sleep in a tent here; you stay here on holiday, like in Pixel Plaza. Challenge a classmate too, then type the hidden word.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: BEACH (book, end, April, camp or campsite, hotel). Fast finishers can write their own hidden-word puzzle for a classmate.

quests.title: Last Day of School
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Ask a partner about the last day of school before the summer holidays: "What did you do?", "How did you feel?", "What did you do after school?" Then answer their questions. Can't remember? Invent it! Useful phrases: "I felt ...", "We played ..." Write 3 sentences about your partner's day.
quests.teacherNote: Check past simple questions with "did" and irregular verbs (went, felt, ate). Near the end of the course, you can switch it to plans for this year's last day with "going to".

quests.title: Carnival Squad Costume
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Choose a group costume for the Carnival parade (or any costume party) with two or three classmates: one theme for everyone, like space, food or superheroes. Each person suggests a theme with a reason; compare them and vote. Then decide who wears what. Useful phrases: "I think ... would be better because ...", "That's funnier than ...", "What if we ...?" Write 4 sentences: your theme, why you chose it and each person's costume.
quests.teacherNote: Many Catalan towns and schools parade in group costumes, so students usually have real ideas. Listen for comparatives (funnier, easier to make) and reasons with "because"; if the vote is a tie, the group must find a compromise theme.

quests.title: Summer Camp Mystery
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Solve this puzzle with a partner. Ana, Biel, Carla and Dani go to four different summer camps: sailing, mountain, art and football. Dani needs a ball at his camp. Biel can't swim and he hates walking up hills. Ana feels sick in high places. Who goes to the sailing camp? Useful phrases: "It can't be ... because ...", "So ... must be at ..." Talk it through in the chat, then type only the name.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: Ana. Dani needs a ball (football), so Biel, who can't swim and hates hills, must be at art camp; Ana avoids high places, so she takes sailing and Carla gets the mountain camp.

quests.title: Saint George's Book Hunt
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Get ready for Saint George's Day (Sant Jordi), when people give books and roses! Ask four classmates to recommend a book, comic or graphic novel, and ask follow-up questions. If the title isn't in English, describe the story instead. Then choose the one you most want to read. Useful phrases: "What's it about?", "It sounds more exciting than ...", "I'd love to read it because ..." Write 4 sentences: the recommendations you got and your choice, with a reason.
quests.teacherNote: The chat blocks words that are not English, so students describe books with Catalan or Spanish titles instead of typing them, which is good practice in explaining things another way. Any kind of reading counts, including comics.

quests.title: Spring or Summer Showdown
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Debate with a partner: which season is better, spring or summer? Compare the weather, food, free time and celebrations, like Saint George's Day or Midsummer. Ask "Why?" after every answer and try to agree on a winner. Useful phrases: "Spring is less ... than summer", "I prefer ... because ...", "That's true, but ..." Write 4 sentences: your partner's opinion, your opinion and your final decision.
quests.teacherNote: Look for comparatives (warmer, less crowded, more relaxing) and reasons. If a pair agrees straight away, one student must defend the other season anyway.

quests.title: Mystery Postcard
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Write a postcard from your dream summer holiday: a beach, a camp, a city or your own town. Describe the weather, what you did yesterday and your plans for tomorrow, but don't name the place! Share it in the nearby chat and ask classmates to guess where you are. Useful phrases: "The weather here is ...", "Yesterday I ...", "Tomorrow I'm going to ..." Write your postcard (4-5 sentences) and say whether a classmate guessed it.
quests.teacherNote: Check the mix of tenses: past simple for yesterday and "going to" for tomorrow. Shy students can whisper the postcard to one classmate instead of posting it in the nearby chat.

quests.title: Beach Clean-Up Crew
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Imagine you and two or three classmates are organising a beach clean-up for the first Saturday of the summer holidays. Agree on a catchy slogan and three persuasive reasons to join. Then each of you tries to convince a classmate from another group to sign up, politely answering any excuses. Useful phrases: "Imagine how the beach would look if ...", "I see your point, but ...", "It only takes ..." Write a short paragraph: your slogan, your best arguments and how the persuading went.
quests.teacherNote: The classmates being persuaded can make up playful excuses to make it harder. In the paragraph, look for second conditionals and polite counter-arguments.

quests.title: The Holiday Compromise
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Plan an imaginary one-week summer trip with a partner, but you want different things. Decide who is A and who is B. A loves the beach, hates long walks and likes sleeping late. B loves the mountains, hates crowds and likes getting up early. Negotiate a plan you both accept: where you go, where you stay and what you do each day. Useful phrases: "I'd be happy to ... as long as ...", "How about a compromise?", "If we ..., then ..." Write a short paragraph summarising your plan and what each of you gave up.
quests.teacherNote: A good paragraph shows that both sides gave something up (e.g. a quiet beach campsite with one day in the mountains). For a harder version, add a twist: it rains for three days.

quests.title: The Long Summer Debate
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Survey at least four classmates: "Should summer holidays be shorter, with more short breaks during the school year?" Ask everyone for a reason, then test their opinion with a "what if" question, like "What if you had two extra weeks off in February?" Useful phrases: "Most people think ...", "Some argued that ..., while others ...", "Personally, I'm not convinced that ..." Write a short paragraph summarising the different views and your own opinion.
quests.teacherNote: This is a real debate in Catalonia, where summer holidays are long. Give credit to reports that sum up both sides fairly before giving their own view, and check reporting language (some argued that..., while others...).

quests.title: Midsummer Night Rules
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Run the Midsummer (Sant Joan) night party in Pixel Plaza with two or three classmates, or another summer festival you like. Some people want fireworks and loud music all night; others worry about noise, frightened pets and rubbish in the park. Agree on three rules that keep the party fun and fair for everyone. Useful phrases: "If we banned ..., people would ...", "On the other hand, ...", "A fair solution would be ..." Write a short paragraph: your three rules and the reasons behind them.
quests.teacherNote: Look for second conditionals and reasons that weigh both sides (fun against noise, pets and litter). Groups can post their rules in the nearby chat and the class can vote for the fairest set.

quests.title: The Dragon's Side
quests.category: Carnival, Saint George's Day, Spring & Summer
quests.text: Retell the Saint George's Day legend from the dragon's point of view. In the usual story, a knight defeats a dragon to save a princess and her town, and a red rose appears. But what if the dragon was misunderstood? Explain, as the dragon, what really happened and how you felt. Then share a short version in the chat and ask two classmates whether the dragon deserves a second chance. Useful phrases: "If only they had listened ...", "I had no choice but to ...", "Nobody ever asked why ..." Write a short paragraph as the dragon, plus one sentence about your classmates' verdict.
quests.teacherNote: Look for narrative tenses and ways of expressing regret (If only..., should have...). Keep it light and funny; the class can vote in the chat for the most convincing dragon.

quests.title: Twenty for the Café
quests.text: Find a classmate who is the café baker. Ask: "How many chestnuts does the café need?" Are you the baker? Tell two classmates the answer. Then type the number.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: 20 (twenty). It comes from the Baker's reward for 'where' ("The café needs 20 chestnuts. That is half of the box."), so at least one baker must have answered 'where' before others can find it.

quests.title: No Chestnuts Today
quests.text: Invite three classmates to your café. Say: "Welcome! Sorry, we have no chestnuts today. Do you want hot chocolate, tea or cake?" Write 2 sentences: "... wants ... ."
quests.teacherNote: Secret mission for bakers only, playing on the missing chestnuts. Check the third person -s in "wants"; stronger students can add "... doesn't want ..." or offer more café items.

quests.title: The Long Ride
quests.text: Find a classmate who is the driver. Ask: "How long is the ride from the shop to the park?" Then ask one more question. Are you the driver? Answer two classmates instead. Useful phrases: "How long does it take?" "It takes ..." Type the answer with a word like "minutes" or "hours".
quests.teacherNote: Answer: 30 minutes (half an hour), from the Driver's reward for 'where' ("The ride from the shop to the park takes 30 minutes."). A bare "30" is not accepted on purpose, because a wrong clock time like "9:30" would also match it.

quests.title: Where Were You?
quests.text: Play detective! Ask four classmates about their character: "Where were you in town at nine o'clock this morning? What did you see?" They can invent a fun answer. Useful phrases: "I was at the ...", "I saw ...". Write 3 sentences: who you asked and what they said.
quests.teacherNote: Answers are invented and in character, so nobody shares real places. Check was/were and past simple (saw, went); as a follow-up, ask the class whether two people 'saw' the same thing.

quests.title: Lost Box Notice
quests.text: Write a "Lost box" notice in nearby chat. Say the box's colour, what is inside and when it left the shop. Ask three classmates: "Did you see this box?" Useful phrases: "Lost: a ... box with ...", "It left the shop at ...". Write your notice and what they said.
quests.teacherNote: Secret mission for shopkeepers, built only on their starting clue (a blue box left the shop at 9:00) plus the obvious fact that it held chestnuts. Check that the notice is clear and that the replies they record use past simple.

quests.title: The Green Coat
quests.text: Talk to a hotel receptionist about the man in the green coat. Ask what time he came to the desk and what he wanted. Then ask a follow-up question, like "Do you think he is important? Why?" Are you the receptionist? Answer a classmate's questions instead. Useful phrases: "What exactly did he ask?" "What makes you say that?" Type the time he asked about the park.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: 9:15 (quarter past nine), from the Receptionist's reward for 'where' ("A man in a green coat asked me about the park at 9:15."). The 'coat' news says a neighbour saw a green coat near the park at 9:20, which is not accepted, so this is a good moment to compare the two times.

quests.title: Front Page News
quests.text: Work with two or three classmates as reporters for the town newspaper. Share what each of you knows about the missing chestnuts; report facts, not guesses. Everyone suggests a headline, then compare them and vote for the best one. Useful phrases: "I prefer ... because ...", "Yours is catchier than mine.", "Shall we choose ...?" Write the winning headline, 3 sentences of news and one reason why your group chose it.
quests.teacherNote: Works at any point in the chapter: early groups report what is still unknown, later groups can add the park and the times. Look for comparatives in the vote and check that the news contains facts, not accusations against classmates.

quests.title: Good News or Bad News?
quests.text: Go to the hotel and read the note on the door. Is it good news or bad news? Discuss with a partner and ask them a follow-up question. Useful phrases: "I think it's good news because...", "I'm not so sure, because...", "Why do you think that?" Write 3-4 sentences: your opinion, your partner's opinion and one reason for each.
quests.teacherNote: The hotel-door discovery says "The chestnuts are safe. Do not worry." Both readings (comforting or suspicious) are valid; reward clear because-clauses and real follow-up questions, not a 'right' opinion.

quests.title: Plan B for the Party
quests.text: Hold an emergency meeting with two or three classmates: the party starts at 6:00, you need the chestnuts before 5:00, and they are still not here. Propose two backup plans (for example, a different snack, a later start or a search team) and persuade the group to choose one. Listen to objections and negotiate a compromise. Useful phrases: "If we ..., we could ...", "I see your point, but ...", "What if we ...?" Write a short paragraph: the options, what each person thought and the final decision with reasons.
quests.teacherNote: Secret mission for planners, built on the Planner's reward for 'where' (party at 6:00, chestnuts needed before 5:00). Look for conditionals, polite disagreement and a summary that includes the classmates' views, not only the planner's.

quests.title: Never Again Rules
quests.text: Meet two or three classmates and make next year's chestnut delivery safer: this year the lock was open and the box was empty! Each person suggests one rule about keys, locks, routes or times. Focus on rules, not on suspects. Discuss the pros and cons of every rule, then agree on the best two. Useful phrases: "If we had ..., this wouldn't have happened.", "The problem with that is ...", "On the other hand, ..." Write a short paragraph summarising the different views and your two final rules.
quests.teacherNote: Use after the chapter ending (two keys, open lock, empty box). Look for third conditionals and a summary that reports more than one view; the 'rules, not suspects' focus keeps the quest fair for every student, including a future thief.

quests.title: Follow the Blue Box
quests.text: Ask classmates: "Where is the blue box?" The driver knows. Then ask: "Where is the water in this town?" Type the place: "The box is near the ..."
quests.teacherNote: Answer: the pond in the park. It comes from the driver's starting clue ('I carried a blue box. I left it near the water.') plus the planner's starting clue ('The only water in town is the pond in the park.'). 'Water' on its own is not accepted, so students have to ask a planner as well as a driver.

quests.title: Clue Swap
quests.text: Find a classmate with a different job. Say: "I am the ... My clue is ..." Ask: "What is your job? What is your clue?" Write 1-2 sentences: "The ... says ..."
quests.teacherNote: Check that the student reports the partner's clue, not their own, e.g. 'The driver says the blue box is near the water.' Stronger A1 students can swap clues with two classmates.

quests.title: Lost Chestnuts Poster
quests.text: Make a LOST poster for the festival chestnuts. Post it in the nearby chat. Then write it here in 2 sentences: "LOST: chestnuts for the festival! Please tell the ... at the ..."
quests.teacherNote: Good answers name a story job and a place, e.g. 'Please tell the baker at the cafe.' Faster students can add a detail from their clues, such as the blue box or a time.

quests.title: The Open Shop Door
quests.text: Find out why the shop door was open at 9:05. Ask a shopkeeper: "Where did you go at 9:05?" Then ask one more question, like "Why didn't you close the door?" Type the answer: "The shopkeeper went to the ..."
quests.teacherNote: Answer: the bank. It comes from the shopkeeper's reward for 'meet-shop' ('At 9:05 I went to the bank. The shop door was open.') and matches the 'door' news. A shopkeeper who has not answered 'meet-shop' yet will not have this line, so tell the student to ask a different shopkeeper.

quests.title: Who Called the Hotel?
quests.text: Find out who called the hotel. Keep this mission secret. You know the hotel phone rang at 9:25 and nobody answered. Ask 3 classmates: "Did you call the hotel?" "Where were you at 9:25?" Write 3 sentences, one for each classmate: "... was at/in the ... at 9:25."
quests.teacherNote: Only receptionists see this. It builds on their starting clue ('The hotel phone rang at 9:25. Nobody answered.'). Look for correct 'was at/in' and past simple questions. Someone may give the thief's cover story ('At 9:25 I was at the hotel desk'). That is part of the game, and the quest never asks anyone to accuse a classmate.

quests.title: The Planner's Morning
quests.text: Interview a festival planner about their morning. Ask where they were at 9:20 and who was with them, then ask two follow-up questions, for example what they were doing and how the party plans are going now. Useful phrases: "Where exactly were you at 9:20?" "What were you doing there?" "How do you feel about the party now?" Type the place where the planner was at 9:20: "At 9:20 the planner was in the ..."
quests.teacherNote: Answer: the square. It comes from the planner's reward for 'meet-shop' ('At 9:20 I was in the square with the band'). 'Fountain' is also accepted because the fountain is in the square. Check the follow-up questions in the chat log, because they show more language than the one-word answer.

quests.title: The Driver's Delivery Log
quests.text: Prepare your secret delivery log. You carried a blue box and left it near the water, but the log needs more details. Ask a shopkeeper what time the box left the shop, ask classmates where the water is, and ask one more classmate what they saw that morning. Useful phrases: "What time did the box leave?" "Are you sure?" "What did you see?" Write 4-5 sentences in time order, then say which detail you are not sure about and why.
quests.teacherNote: Only drivers see this. A complete log includes 9:00 (shopkeeper's starting clue), the pond in the park (planner's starting clue) and one more witness detail, with sequencers like 'first', 'then', 'after that'. The 'not sure' sentence should give a reason.

quests.title: Breaking Festival News
quests.text: Report the festival morning for the town newspaper. Interview two classmates with different jobs: ask what they did or saw between 9:00 and 9:30, and ask each one a follow-up question. Report only what people said and do not accuse anyone. Useful phrases: "According to the baker, ..." "Both of them said ..." "Nobody knows yet why ..." Write a headline and 3-4 sentences: what each person said and whether their stories agree.
quests.teacherNote: Look for reporting verbs ('said', 'told me'), a short factual headline and a clear comparison of the two stories. If you have already shown the news, students can also mention that the shop door was open at 9:05 or that the hotel phone rang at 9:25.

quests.title: One Box, Two Stories
quests.text: Settle an argument between the cafe and the shop: they tell different stories about a blue box. Pair up with a classmate who has the other job (baker with shopkeeper) and compare your clues. Suggest at least two explanations that would make both of you right, then negotiate which is most likely. Useful phrases: "Suppose the box never..." "That would explain why..." "I'd accept that, as long as..." Write a short paragraph: both claims, your explanations, the one you agreed on and what you would ask the driver next.
quests.teacherNote: Only bakers and shopkeepers see this. Their starting clues are 'A blue box left the shop at 9:00' and 'No blue box came to the cafe'. A strong paragraph shows that both can be true, for example because the box went somewhere else (the driver left it near the water), and uses conditionals to compare the explanations.

quests.title: Why Take the Chestnuts?
quests.text: Discuss the big question that is still open: why would someone take the festival chestnuts? With 2-3 classmates, suggest at least three possible motives, then challenge each other: which is most likely, and what evidence would you need? Finally, imagine you were the thief: how would you make things right before the party? Keep it kind; it is only a game role, so say "the thief", never a classmate's name. Useful phrases: "They might have wanted to..." "That seems unlikely because..." "If I were them, I would..." Write a short paragraph summarising the different views and the one your group finds most convincing.
quests.teacherNote: It unlocks after the chapter is solved and builds on the ending question ('But why did they take the chestnuts?'). The chapter does not answer that question, so every idea is a guess. Look for modal speculation ('might have', 'can't have', 'must have') and a balanced summary. The student who played the thief can take part like everyone else.

quests.title: The Heavy Bag
quests.text: Find a driver and ask: "What time does the heavy bag go to the hotel?" Say "Thank you!" Are you a driver? Ask another driver. Type the time.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: 9:40. It comes from the driver's chapter 3 starting clue ("At 9:40 I carried a heavy bag to the hotel.") and also from the teacher news 'bag'. Digit and word forms are accepted (9:40, 9.40, nine forty, twenty to ten).

quests.title: Truck Number Hunt
quests.text: Find a driver and ask: "What is the number of your truck?" The driver answers: "My truck is number ..." It is one number of the door code. Type the number.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: 7. It is the driver's reward for 'hide' ("One number of the code is 7. It is the number of my truck."). A driver who has not answered 'hide' yet will not know it, so the student should try another driver.

quests.title: Haunted Party Snacks
quests.text: Help the town plan food for the haunted party. Ask three classmates: "What food do you like at a party?" Write two sentences, for example: "Leo likes pizza. Mia and Sam like hot chestnuts."
quests.teacherNote: Check the third-person -s (he likes, they like). Students who are stuck can use festival food such as hot chestnuts, sweet potatoes or cakes.

quests.title: Who Signed It?
quests.text: Find a festival planner and ask: "Who signed the note in the cellar?" Are you a planner? Ask another planner. Then ask a classmate with a different role: "What does your part of the note say?" Type who signed the note.
quests.teacherNote: Answer: a friend of the town. It is the planner's reward for 'code' ("The note is signed by a friend of the town."). Any answer that contains the word friend is accepted. A planner who has not answered 'code' yet will not know it, so the student should try another planner.

quests.title: Hotel Desk Survey
quests.text: Welcome four classmates to your hotel. Strange things are happening there! Ask each guest: "Did you see or smell anything strange near the hotel today?" Useful phrases: "Welcome to the hotel!", "Thank you for your help." Write 3 sentences: who you asked and what they said.
quests.teacherNote: Only receptionists see this. Look for past simple questions (Did you see...?) and short reported answers (She said she smelled chestnuts). Bakers and drivers have hotel clues, so they have something real to say.

quests.title: Town Gossip
quests.text: Share town gossip! Tell three classmates one thing from your clue. Listen to their news too. Useful phrases: "Did you hear about...?", "I heard that...", "Really? Who told you?" Write 3 sentences about what you heard, for example: "The shopkeeper told me that..."
quests.teacherNote: Good at the start of a session: each role has a different clue, so everyone hears something new. Look for "told me that" and "I heard that", and remind students to share hints, not answers.

quests.title: Secret Timeline
quests.text: Find a classmate with the other role (driver or shopkeeper) and whisper your clues to each other. Put the two events in time order. Then discuss: what do the clues say about the chestnuts and the thief's plan? Useful phrases: "First..., then...", "It might mean that...", "I agree, but..." Write 3-5 sentences: your timeline and your theory.
quests.teacherNote: Only drivers and shopkeepers see this. Expected timeline: at 9:00 someone bought wood and matches (shopkeeper's clue), and at 9:40 a heavy bag went to the hotel (driver's clue). Good theories connect fire for roasting with the hotel and use might/could.

quests.title: Haunted Party Poster
quests.text: Work with two or three classmates to plan a poster for the haunted chestnut party. Find a festival planner to check the start time. Agree on a place in town, food, games and costumes, and add one idea from another celebration you like. Useful phrases: "What about...?", "I prefer... because...", "Let's go with..." Write the poster text in 3-5 sentences.
quests.teacherNote: The party starts at 6:00 (the planner's starting clue), so the best posters include that time. Look for suggestions with reasons. Groups can post their poster text in nearby chat and the class can vote.

quests.title: Plan B Party
quests.text: Save the party! It starts at 6:00 and the chestnuts are still missing. Persuade at least four classmates to help with a Plan B in case the chestnuts are not found in time. Listen to their ideas, answer their doubts and give each person a job, such as cooking, music or decorations. Useful phrases: "If we can't find them, we could...", "Would you be willing to...?", "I see your point, but..." Write a short paragraph: summarise the plan, who agreed to do what, and one objection you dealt with.
quests.teacherNote: Only festival planners see this. Look for conditionals and polite persuasion. A strong paragraph names at least three jobs and explains how one doubt was solved. If the class has already found the chestnuts, treat it as a backup plan for next year.

quests.title: Front Page Story
quests.text: Report the big story for the town newspaper! Interview two classmates with different roles: how did they help find the chestnuts, and was the surprise party plan a good idea? Call the person who hid the chestnuts "a friend of the town", not by name. Useful phrases: "According to...", "...admitted that...", "while others felt that..." Write a headline and a short paragraph that summarises the night, quotes both people and compares their views.
quests.teacherNote: Use this after the chapter is solved. Check the reporting verbs and that both opinions appear. The "friend of the town" rule (from the signed note) keeps the student who played the thief from being singled out.
